items.title: Meet the 52 women competing to be the next Miss America
items.summary: Contestants for the coming Miss America pageant. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. The next Miss America will be crowned on September 6 in West Palm Beach. More than 50 women will be competing for the title this year. The contestants include a medical student, a professional ballroom dancer, and a karate instructor. It's almost time to crown the next Miss America . On September 6, 52 women from around the country will gather at the Palm Beach County Convention Center in West Palm Beach, Florida, for the chance to win the coveted title. The winner will be crowned by Miss America 2026 Cassie Donnegan and will take home a $50,000 scholarship. Before you watch the competition — which will stream on PageantVision.com at 7 p.m. ET — meet the 52 women competing for the crown . Alabama: Ruby Tilghman Miss Alabama. Courtesy of Miss America IP INC. Ruby Tilghman, 22, graduated from the University of Alabama with a degree in chemistry. She is an incoming student at the university's Heersink School of Medicine. Tilghman previously represented Florida at the Miss America's Teen competition in 2021. Tilghman is an avid hiker who has visited 28 national parks. She is also a recipient of the President's Volunteer Service Lifetime Achievement Award. Alaska: Nora Andrews Miss Alaska. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Nora Andrews, 20, is a senior at Grand Canyon University, where she is studying psychology and professional writing. She is hoping to earn a Ph.D. in clinical psychology and a certification in sex and relational education and therapy. Andrews is also an advocate for suicide prevention and mental health awareness. Arizona: Victoria Vredevoogd Miss Arizona. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Victoria Vredevoogd, 25, is a law student at the Sandra Day O'Connor College of Law at Arizona State University. The pageant queen founded and serves as president of The Gender Violence Project, an organization at ASU that advocates for survivors and provides free legal resources. She also wrote and published her own fantasy novel, titled "A Legend of Golden Shadows." Arkansas: Ava Weeks Miss Arkansas. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Ava Weeks, 20, is a student at Ouachita Baptist University. She hopes to become a secondary English teacher. Weeks became an advocate for passenger safety after witnessing a terrible car accident when she was a teenager, according to her Miss America bio. Her community initiative is "Every Seat. Every Ride. Buckle Up." Weeks has won over $50,000 in scholarships from competing in the Miss America system. California: Sharlize True Trujillo Miss California. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Sharlize True Trujillo, 22, is pursuing a degree in gender studies and a minor in film and television from the University of California, Los Angeles. She is planning to attend law school and study entertainment law. The pageant queen is also a dancer, actress, and content creator. She has more than 2 million followers on TikTok. Colorado: Gabrielle Burns Miss Colorado. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Gabrielle Burns, 23, is pursuing a master's degree from the University of Colorado Boulder. She is studying to become a speech-language pathologist. Burns is an advocate for communication disorders and disabilities. She's also a professional ballroom dancer. Connecticut: Christa Steiner Miss Connecticut. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Christa Steiner, 27, graduated from the Manhattan School of Music, where she earned a degree in vocal performance and musical theater. Steiner is a professional singer and voice teacher. She is using her Miss America platform to advocate for increased access to mental health treatment. Delaware: Anaya Harrison Miss Delaware. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Anaya Harrison, 24, earned both her undergraduate and graduate degrees from the Biden School of Public Policy at the University of Delaware. She plans to attend law school. Harrison works as a congressional aide in the US House of Representatives, where she "helps constituents navigate federal agencies," according to her Miss America bio. District of Columbia: Evelyn Smith Miss District of Columbia. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Evelyn Smith, 25, graduated from Oklahoma City University with a bachelor's degree in philosophy and minors in political science and studio art. She was the first Black woman to win Miss Oklahoma's Teen, and she made it to the top nine at the Miss America's Teen 2018 competition. Smith has certified more than 1,000 individuals in CPR. She used her own skills to save her mother's life during a heart attack, according to her Miss America bio. Florida: Alexandra de Roos Miss Florida. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Alexandra de Roos, 23, is an honors student at the University of South Florida, where she is studying psychology. She plans to attend medical school and become a neuropsychiatrist. The pageant queen was previously a student at the School of American Ballet, but her dancing career was cut short after a traumatic brain injury. She founded The Blue Project nonprofit to advocate for brain injury education and healing through the arts, according to her Miss Florida bio. Georgia: Sophia Wootten Miss Georgia. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Sophia Wootten, 21, is pursuing a degree in communication sciences and disorders at the University of Georgia. She is planning to become a pediatric audiologist. Wootten made history as the first Miss America contestant with a cleft lip and palate. She has undergone 20 reconstructive surgeries and wears hearing aids. The pageant queen wants to use her platform to "redefine what representation looks like for children with disabilities," according to her Miss America bio. Hawaii: Carly Yoshida Miss Hawaii. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Carly Yoshida, 26, earned a degree in social sciences from the University of Hawai'i - West O'ahu and plans to pursue a professional meteorology degree. Yoshida is a field reporter, digital content producer, and on-air weather personality for KITV 4 Island News, an ABC affiliate in Honolulu. She previously won Miss Hawaii's Teen in 2016. Idaho: Déja Fitzwater Miss Idaho. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Déja Fitzwater, 21, is studying communications at the University of Idaho. She is an avid 4-H volunteer and won Miss Oregon's Teen in 2022. Fitzwater, an advocate for agricultural literacy, is using her platform to "help young people better understand the people, science, and industries behind their food and natural resources," according to her Miss America bio. Illinois: Kate Dimmett Miss Illinois. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Kate Dimmett, 23, graduated from both the Kelley School of Business and the Jacobs School of Music at Indiana University. The pageant queen is a professional violinist. Dimmett is the president of Notable Measures, a nonprofit she launched at 13 to expand access to music education. According to her Miss America bio, she has raised over $90,000 and provided 170 grants through her organization. She previously won Miss Indiana's Teen in 2021. Indiana: Ellise Edwards Miss Indiana. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Ellise Edwards, 22, graduated from the University of South Florida. She is a content creator with over 127,000 followers on TikTok, where she shares videos of her curly-hair routine and her experience as a postgrad. Edwards wants to help businesses grow their online presence "through strategic social media marketing," according to her Miss America bio. Iowa: McKenzie Kerry Miss Iowa. Contestants for the coming Miss America pageant.

Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC.

  • The next Miss America will be crowned on September 6 in West Palm Beach.
  • More than 50 women will be competing for the title this year.
  • The contestants include a medical student, a professional ballroom dancer, and a karate instructor.

It's almost time to crown the next Miss America.

On September 6, 52 women from around the country will gather at the Palm Beach County Convention Center in West Palm Beach, Florida, for the chance to win the coveted title.

The winner will be crowned by Miss America 2026 Cassie Donnegan and will take home a $50,000 scholarship.

Before you watch the competition — which will stream on PageantVision.com at 7 p.m. ET — meet the 52 women competing for the crown.

Alabama: Ruby Tilghman
Miss Alabama.

Courtesy of Miss America IP INC.

Ruby Tilghman, 22, graduated from the University of Alabama with a degree in chemistry. She is an incoming student at the university's Heersink School of Medicine. Tilghman previously represented Florida at the Miss America's Teen competition in 2021.

Tilghman is an avid hiker who has visited 28 national parks. She is also a recipient of the President's Volunteer Service Lifetime Achievement Award.

Alaska: Nora Andrews
Miss Alaska.

Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC.

Andrews is also an advocate for suicide prevention and mental health awareness.

Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC.

items.title: TikTok Announces Four New Comment Features Including Voice Comments and Polls
items.summary: TikTok has revealed that it will be introducing four new features to the comment section over the coming month, such as voice comments and polls. These features are being introduced at different times, with a few of them available this week and the rest coming next month. The new features make the comments more visual and interactive by including audio comments of up to 60 seconds, polls with up to five options, Live Photos, and multi-photo carousels. Text and photo comments are still available. Thursday, TikTok revealed the features. TikTok Adds Voice Comments, Polls, and Live Photos From next month, TikTok will be offering voice comments that can last up to 60 seconds. According to TikTok's press release, users will be able to attach a text comment to a voice comment, just as is the case with photo comments. This means that in addition to the existing options of text and photo, audio comments will now be available as well. From this week onwards, creators will be able to include polls in the comments section of their videos, with each poll having up to five possible voting options. They can decide how long the voting will continue for and will be able to see the votes as they happen. This could be useful for creators of all sizes who want to get feedback from their viewers, providing an alternative to asking for people's opinions directly in the comments. TikTok has now added the option to include Live Photos in comments, alongside static images. Since users are already familiar with the ability to add GIFs to comments, it is not clear how extensively Live Photo comments will be used. TikTok Photo Carousels in Comments TikTok is developing the ability for users to include up to nine photos in a single comment. Just as with regular carousels, viewers will be able to swipe through the photos, even when using the full-screen view. The feature will be rolled out during the course of the month. The four features are being introduced at different times. Polls are being launched this week, voice comments will come next month and photo carousels will be introduced over the course of the month. Support for Live Photos is said to be currently available. It does not state whether the rollouts are carried out by region or by platform, so availability might differ from account to account as TikTok introduces each feature. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. The post TikTok Announces Four New Comment Features Including Voice Comments and Polls appeared first on gHacks .

items.title: I’m dating a founder and it feels like a relationship on steroids. I’ve had to take a backseat to my dreams— but with the right person, it’s worth it.
items.summary: Maria Diaz Valdez and her partner Emil. Maria Diaz Valdez Maria Diaz Valdez has been dating her partner, Emil, since he became a founder about four years ago. She says she put her dreams on the back burner to help him grow, but she knows it will be worth it. Diaz Valdez says dating a founder requires a strong sense of self, boundaries, and a support system. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Maria Diaz Valdez, a 29-year-old based in Spain. It's been edited for length and clarity. I feel like a relationship with a founder is a relationship on steroids because it's so intense in the trust and patience it requires. I've had to be committed to his journey, but I'm not in charge of it, and that's very scary. My partner, Emil, and I met as roommates in a shared household in Norway, and we've been together for four years. I was lucky enough to get to know him so well as a friend before we started dating because we had all sorts of honest conversations about our goals without trying to impress each other. That level of honesty and communication has been the foundation of everything we've built in our relationship. It's been strange to take a backseat role to build my career to help him build his, and there are times we feel more like business partners than life partners, but I'm in this for the long haul. I trust this journey, and I know he'll support me the same way as I build my own entrepreneurial journey. We created a contract toward the start of our relationship Emil didn't start his current entrepreneurial journey until right before we started dating, so I've kind of been through everything with him. I was even his first client. I was building a jewelry brand at the time and hired him to help me develop my website. At the start of our relationship, we had a lot of conversations about his vision for the company, my role in it, and whether he saw this future with me. Our discussions made me feel confident that he'd actually pursue his goals, but I still had to put a lot of trust in him. I lent him money those first couple of months, which was scary, but I believed in him. We wrote a contract that tracked the money I was sending him and established a deal that there would come a day when he'd need to support me in return. I've had to take a backseat to his dreams, but I know he'll return the favor I've always been a career person — someone with direction who works very hard. Now I'm with someone who's outperforming me in that area. I'm not blindly trusting everything will go well; we have conversations about this constantly. It's strange, but it's a conscious choice I've made because I view this person as somebody I want to experience my whole life with. I write a lot in my diary, trying to figure out what I truly feel and want. The biggest challenge to wrap my head around is that his passion and project are taking priority, and I must remember that things will change as I figure out what I'm most passionate about. Emil and I have very compatible skills and knowledge; I focus on design, marketing, and branding, while he is in tech and business development. With his help, I've even started creating my marketing platform, CrazeAI. Work sometimes comes before the relationship, so we focus on presence with each other Emil is the type of person who really values quality time. If we watch something on Netflix, for example, we're not going to be on our phones. We're in this together. I think we're very conscious of the distractions we have around us. Because of that, I'm very lenient in times when he has to step away for something at work. There are times we'll be on a walk together, and one of his partners calls, and he suddenly forgets he's on a walk with me. He'll just walk away. Diaz Valdez and Emil make time away from work to be fully present with each other. Maria Diaz Valdez I don't worry about it too much because I've been in that position before. When I was building the jewelry brand , I would wake up in the middle of the night having to answer emails. I have a lot of understanding that he's in a position where these moments can make it or break it for his business. Our baseline is one of presence, so when something comes up, it's OK. Most of our conversations go back to business It's very hard not to talk about the development of the business because that's the stage we're in. We're both very passionate about it, and we work together on it, so it doesn't feel like a dragging conversation. There are times we go out to have a drink and try not to talk about business , but then we start dreaming and saying things like "Imagine when we get to this level or through these things." It feels supportive to talk through these things. We also try to play chess every once in a while and take salsa classes. That's a time when we're not talking or thinking about work at all. We set aside moments to remind each other we're life partners, not business partners We're often in a mode where we have to buckle down and figure issues out about the business, and those conversations aren't happening in a candlelit dinner setting. We're sitting down with an Excel sheet, sourcing out financials. It's not very romantic. Recently, we've been trying to get out of our usual environment , whether for a day trip, a hike, or a trip back home to Norway to see family, to remind us that we have identities outside of being a doer and fixer. That's when we usually find each other again and remember, "Oh wait, I'm also a girlfriend." I'm also very persistent about spending two minutes before we go to bed without distractions to just be together and settle. It's very important to have routines like that. You need a strong sense of self to date a founder If you're entering a relationship with a founder, you need your own strong support system and lifestyle. Your whole life cannot be the relationship, because it's not theirs. Founders can be so focused on chasing their dream that they can forget your needs or your dates. You need to have your own life so those moments don't feel too heavy, and find a balance between forgiveness and setting boundaries. Founders are dreamers, and they often dream about what their life will look like when their business succeeds. Are you a part of that dream? Are they saying "when we get to that point.." or is it "when I get to that point.."? Little things like that are so important. We dream a lot together, so I know his success is my success. Do you have a story to share about what it's like to date a founder? If so, please reach out to the editor, Manseen Logan, at mlogan@businessinsider.com. Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Maria Diaz Valdez and her partner Emil.

Maria Diaz Valdez

  • Maria Diaz Valdez has been dating her partner, Emil, since he became a founder about four years ago.
  • She says she put her dreams on the back burner to help him grow, but she knows it will be worth it.
  • Diaz Valdez says dating a founder requires a strong sense of self, boundaries, and a support system.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Maria Diaz Valdez, a 29-year-old based in Spain. It's been edited for length and clarity.

I feel like a relationship with a founder is a relationship on steroids because it's so intense in the trust and patience it requires. I've had to be committed to his journey, but I'm not in charge of it, and that's very scary.

My partner, Emil, and I met as roommates in a shared household in Norway, and we've been together for four years. I was lucky enough to get to know him so well as a friend before we started dating because we had all sorts of honest conversations about our goals without trying to impress each other. That level of honesty and communication has been the foundation of everything we've built in our relationship.

It's been strange to take a backseat role to build my career to help him build his, and there are times we feel more like business partners than life partners, but I'm in this for the long haul. I trust this journey, and I know he'll support me the same way as I build my own entrepreneurial journey.

We created a contract toward the start of our relationship

Emil didn't start his current entrepreneurial journey until right before we started dating, so I've kind of been through everything with him. I was even his first client. I was building a jewelry brand at the time and hired him to help me develop my website.

At the start of our relationship, we had a lot of conversations about his vision for the company, my role in it, and whether he saw this future with me. Our discussions made me feel confident that he'd actually pursue his goals, but I still had to put a lot of trust in him. I lent him money those first couple of months, which was scary, but I believed in him.

We wrote a contract that tracked the money I was sending him and established a deal that there would come a day when he'd need to support me in return.

I've had to take a backseat to his dreams, but I know he'll return the favor

I've always been a career person — someone with direction who works very hard. Now I'm with someone who's outperforming me in that area. I'm not blindly trusting everything will go well; we have conversations about this constantly.

It's strange, but it's a conscious choice I've made because I view this person as somebody I want to experience my whole life with. I write a lot in my diary, trying to figure out what I truly feel and want. The biggest challenge to wrap my head around is that his passion and project are taking priority, and I must remember that things will change as I figure out what I'm most passionate about.

Emil and I have very compatible skills and knowledge; I focus on design, marketing, and branding, while he is in tech and business development. With his help, I've even started creating my marketing platform, CrazeAI.

Work sometimes comes before the relationship, so we focus on presence with each other

Emil is the type of person who really values quality time. If we watch something on Netflix, for example, we're not going to be on our phones. We're in this together. I think we're very conscious of the distractions we have around us.

Because of that, I'm very lenient in times when he has to step away for something at work. There are times we'll be on a walk together, and one of his partners calls, and he suddenly forgets he's on a walk with me. He'll just walk away.

Diaz Valdez and Emil make time away from work to be fully present with each other.

Maria Diaz Valdez

I don't worry about it too much because I've been in that position before. When I was building the jewelry brand, I would wake up in the middle of the night having to answer emails. I have a lot of understanding that he's in a position where these moments can make it or break it for his business.

Our baseline is one of presence, so when something comes up, it's OK.

Most of our conversations go back to business

It's very hard not to talk about the development of the business because that's the stage we're in. We're both very passionate about it, and we work together on it, so it doesn't feel like a dragging conversation.

There are times we go out to have a drink and try not to talk about business, but then we start dreaming and saying things like "Imagine when we get to this level or through these things." It feels supportive to talk through these things.

We also try to play chess every once in a while and take salsa classes. That's a time when we're not talking or thinking about work at all.

We set aside moments to remind each other we're life partners, not business partners

We're often in a mode where we have to buckle down and figure issues out about the business, and those conversations aren't happening in a candlelit dinner setting. We're sitting down with an Excel sheet, sourcing out financials. It's not very romantic.

Recently, we've been trying to get out of our usual environment, whether for a day trip, a hike, or a trip back home to Norway to see family, to remind us that we have identities outside of being a doer and fixer. That's when we usually find each other again and remember, "Oh wait, I'm also a girlfriend."

I'm also very persistent about spending two minutes before we go to bed without distractions to just be together and settle. It's very important to have routines like that.

You need a strong sense of self to date a founder

If you're entering a relationship with a founder, you need your own strong support system and lifestyle. Your whole life cannot be the relationship, because it's not theirs.

Founders can be so focused on chasing their dream that they can forget your needs or your dates. You need to have your own life so those moments don't feel too heavy, and find a balance between forgiveness and setting boundaries.

Founders are dreamers, and they often dream about what their life will look like when their business succeeds. Are you a part of that dream? Are they saying "when we get to that point.." or is it "when I get to that point.."? Little things like that are so important.

We dream a lot together, so I know his success is my success.

items.title: Tesla Launches Cybercab Robotaxi Rides in Austin With a 45-Vehicle Fleet
items.summary: Tesla has introduced its Cybercab robotaxi and is offering it to customers via its Robotaxi app, with availability at first limited to Austin, Texas. The Cybercab was officially launched on Thursday. It has been designed from the beginning for autonomous travel and includes no steering wheel or pedals. The New York Times states that there are only 45 Cybercabs in the Tesla fleet based in Austin, the fleet comprising a total of 314 vehicles. While the Cybercab cannot be bought by individuals, Tesla has set up an interest form for potential fleet buyers. Tesla's larger Robotaxi fleet also includes Model Ys and Robovans in several cities. Tesla Cybercab Availability and Steering-Wheel-Free Design The Robotaxi fleet operated by Tesla includes Model Ys, Robovans, and is now also made up of Cybercabs, with services available in Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, and Tampa; the Cybercab, though, seems to be available only in Austin, and Tesla made this clear by posting on X that "the future has arrived in Austin". The New York Times states that the Cybercabs in Austin lack a steering wheel and that there are 45 of them in the city's fleet of 314 vehicles. The Cybercab, which was first announced in 2024, is without a steering wheel or pedals and therefore cannot be driven manually in the way that a normal car can; it is intended for use in autonomous journeys. Sawyer Merritt, a fan of Tesla, uploaded videos to X of his first trip in a Cybercab, in which the cabin had two seats and included a big display with no driving controls designed for a person. "The cabin is comfortable and spacious, the suspension is soft, and FSD is VERY smooth. It's an incredible vehicle. The screen is HUGE," he wrote. Tesla Cybercab Fleet Sales and Austin Rollout A Cybercab cannot be purchased by individuals. Tesla has launched an interest form for Robotaxi vehicles as it prepares to sell them to fleet buyers who wish to set up their own Robotaxi networks. Therefore, the Cybercab is being positioned as a vehicle for fleet operators rather than one for individual consumers. The Cybercab is now available via Tesla's Robotaxi app, but only in Austin, there being 45 vehicles in the initial fleet. It has not specified when the Cybercab will be extended to the other Robotaxi cities or when sales of the fleet will start. Tesla has not provided a timeline for scaling up the Cybercab beyond the first deployment in Austin. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. items.title: Google Adds Gemini Voice Features to Gmail, Docs, and Keep for Hands-Free Tasks
items.summary: Google is introducing new voice features powered by Gemini for Gmail, Docs, and Keep, allowing users to carry out tasks by speaking, as stated in a Google announcement. The apps are given new features that make use of the Gemini Audio models, with Gmail introducing conversational inbox search, Docs receiving the ability to draft documents without having to use their hands, and Keep bringing in voice-driven note organisation. This week, the new features will be made available to subscribers of Google AI Plus, Pro, and Ultra. Business customers using Workspace will receive them shortly, too. It all depends on the product. Google demonstrated its Gemini Audio models for the first time at its I/O event in Workspace. Google Gemini Live Features for Gmail, Docs, and Keep Gmail Live is introducing conversational search to the inbox. Rather than having to go through the threads manually, users can pose questions like "What is my flight's gate number?" or "What is happening at my kid's school this week?" and Gmail Live will search through the inbox to give the answers. With Docs Live users are able to create documents by using speech. The tool can arrange their ideas, give the document a structure, and if permitted, retrieve information from Gmail, Drive, Chat, and the web. Google states that it helps users reach a first draft more quickly and also aids in adjusting the tone. With Keep Live, users are able to talk their way through the process of capturing, organizing, and improving their ideas so that they end up with structured and actionable notes. This builds on Keep's normal function of making quick notes by converting spoken brain dumps into structured notes. This week the features are being rolled out. items.title: My kids started school last week, and I pulled them out after the first day for a family trip. I don't regret it.
items.summary: The author says taking her kids out of school just after it started for a family trip was worth it. Courtesy of Kris Ann Valdez I pulled my three kids out of school during the first week of the year for a family trip. They missed only two days of in-person classes and learned about history, nature, and family. I didn't make the decision lightly. I believe some things are worth a few days away from school. I planned a road trip to attend my brother's baby shower in Corona, California, the same week my three kids — entering preschool, third grade, and eighth grade — started school. Since I'm based in Phoenix and my brother lives about 6.5 hours away, driving there is a commitment. I wanted to make the trip count by tacking on some beach time and adventuring, too. I debated the decision. The author took her kids out of school for a family trip. Courtesy of Kris Ann Valdez School started on a Tuesday. My kids attended the first day, then I pulled them out on Wednesday morning to drive to California, with plans to return late Monday evening. Since they attend a hybrid school and learn from home on Fridays and Mondays, they only had to miss two days of in-person learning. Still, I debated it. Those first few days of school are important for establishing routines and setting the tone for the year. But ultimately, I decided to let them miss two days. I'm far from the only parent willing to make that trade-off. A new survey of 1,000 parents found that 91% of parents would or have pulled their kids out of school to travel. More than a quarter (28%) said it's just as educational as traditional classroom time, while 44% said missing a few days is worth it for the meaningful family time. And I wholeheartedly agree. The Channel Islands were our first stop. They explored the Channel Islands. Courtesy of Kris Ann Valdez While researching for this trip, I discovered Channel Islands National Park off the coast of Ventura, an island chain sometimes referred to as "Galapagos of the West" because of its unique wildlife, including the little red island foxes found nowhere else in the world. The islands are also connected to one of my favorite books from when I was growing up, "Island of the Blue Dolphins" by Scott O' Dell. Before we left, my daughter read O' Dell's book, and I told her the account of Juana Maria (also known as the Lone Woman of San Nicolas Island), the Nicoleño Native American woman who inspired the story. We took an hour-ish boat ride to the islands and stood at the bow nearly the entire time, watching for whales and sharks. We didn't see either, but two pods of dolphins swam up to the boat. We saw dolphins from our boat and enjoyed a long hike. They enjoyed a long hike and saw dolphins while on a boat ride. Courtesy of Kris Ann Valdez Once on the island, my third grader was fascinated by the information about the Nicoleño people in the visitor center because she'd just finished the book. My older son, meanwhile, was thoroughly entertained by the Island Scrub-Jay, a rare blue bird found only on the island of Santa Cruz. He loved giving me a play-by-play of what one was doing, marveling that the birds are native to the islands. We also talked with other visitors from around the world and hiked two miles — a lesson in endurance and observing the natural world . We visited other coastal cities, too. They visited Godmother's, a bookstore in Montecito. Courtesy of Kris Ann Valdez After the islands, my husband flew in to join the trip, and we headed for Santa Barbara for a day. As we walked around, we talked about the city's Spanish architecture, the history of colonization, and the California mission system. Connecting our visit back to the Lone Woman, who was eventually brought to Santa Barbara after living alone on San Nicolas Island for 18 years, but died only about seven weeks later, opened up another conversation about the devastating effects European diseases had on Indigenous populations. In nearby Montecito, we visited Godmother's, a charming bookstore where we settled into the children's section to read about another local woman who cleaned up a beach daily and inspired others to do the same, a lesson on how small actions can protect the environment. The baby shower itself was important, too. Showing up for our family, celebrating together, and staying to clean up afterward modeled to our kids that this is how we "do" relationships. Afterward, we drove to Huntington Beach , known as Surf City USA, for two nights, where my eldest son took a surf lesson. Watching him catch waves and learn a new skill felt surreal. I'll keep pulling my kids out of school for experiences like these. The author says she doesn't take missing school lightly, but the trip was worth it. Courtesy of Kris Ann Valdez Yes, my kids missed two days of traditional classroom learning. In exchange, they connected literature to real life, learned about history, encountered wildlife found nowhere else in the world, persevered through a long (by their standards) hike, and learned to surf. I don't take missing school lightly. But for moments like these? It's worth it. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Influencers are infiltrating this year's US Open. It's not stopping tennis lovers.
items.summary: Garrett Ellwood/USTA via Getty Images This post originally appeared in the BI Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . More than tennis 🎾 The US Open has long morphed from a simple tennis tournament into a two-week experience in one of the best boroughs in New York. With merch drops, celebrities in the stands , and viral food items on-site with eye-popping price tags, it's become the social event of September in New York. This year, which runs til September 13, is no exception, despite the drama at the suite level inside Arthur Ashe Stadium. Influencers, some of whom are being paid six figures to recap the US Open, have turned the tournament into a high-stakes, high-payout event. On Monday, a few were spotted inside a suite, ring lights in hand, creating content. It disrupted the match between Naomi Osaka and Anastasia Zakharova so much that by Wednesday, a sign had been posted on the grounds telling onlookers, "Please refrain from the use of flash photography or other lighting." Brendan McIntyre, a spokesperson for the US Open, told me that they're excited a lot of "new fans" are attending the tennis tournament, but want to remind attendees that they shouldn't "interfere with the action and competition on the court." McIntyre added that despite what you've seen on social media, disruptions haven't happened a lot throughout the Open. Either way, it hasn't deterred tennis lovers from making the trek to the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center in droves. BI was also on-site, detailing the best of what the tournament has to offer — aside from seeing our favorite players, of course. We stopped by every single retail store to ask store clerks what the most popular items were, and I chose my favorite ; we stopped by the Heineken suite to see the iconic black and silver outfit Serena Williams wore in 2022 on display; we tried the $38 sandwich attendees can't stop ordering; and watched while a billionaire heiress volleyed for a chance to win her first US Open. And the fun continues next week. See ya in Queens! Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: A veteran chief engineer building a flying taxi shared the one piece of advice he'd give his 25-year-old self
items.summary: David King, and the seats for Vertical Aerospace's air taxi. Pete Syme/Business Insider Vertical Aerospace's chief engineer says he'd tell his younger self to "discover and embrace the discovery." David King said it's important to embrace learning new things and not be afraid of the unknown. It's a handy perspective for the air-taxi firm, which performed the first public transition flight. David King is the chief engineer at Vertical Aerospace , a British company developing an eVTOL — an electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft — intended to work like a flying taxi . If he could give his 25-year-old self one piece of advice, King said, it would be: "Don't be afraid of the unknown." "Just discover, and embrace the discovery, and learn as you go, but get to discovery safely and effectively," he told Business Insider. King, who has more than 35 years of experience in aerospace, spoke to Business Insider at July's Farnborough Airshow , where Vertical's VX4 prototype became the first eVTOL to publicly perform a transition flight. Its wing-mounted propellers tilted so it could fly like an airplane, before transitioning back to land like a helicopter. King began his career after earning a graduate degree from MIT in 1989. He later became the chief engineer on programs at Bell and Leonardo before joining Vertical in 2023. Looking back, he said he had come to appreciate "how much of a rewarding experience it is to learn something new every day." That's a handy perspective for a company building a new type of aircraft. eVTOLs are designed to function like helicopters but make much less noise, so the hope is they could be used over cities more frequently. Vertical Aerospace's air taxi, Valo, on display in London last year. Pete Syme/Business Insider The goal is to transform commutes and other short trips. For example, Vertical says its Valo air taxi could fly the 22 miles from Miami Airport to Fort Lauderdale in 11 minutes, compared to an hour by car. Most manufacturers have said they expect a seat on board to cost about the same as a luxury rideshare option like an Uber Black . However, there is still work to be done for air taxis to be certified by aviation regulators. "When you test it at the next higher level of integration, you're going to have some level of discovery," King said. "Get there quickly, then you learn, adjust your models, and then go test it." For King, the key is making those discoveries without taking unnecessary risks. He said young engineers should put "guardrails" around testing so that they can learn safely, but move quickly enough to avoid becoming stuck trying to make a model perfect before testing it. He recalled getting discouraged by unexpected results when he was younger, but embracing this has been a huge help. "Once people get energized by discovery as opposed to discouraged by discovery, you can see the iterations happen quickly," he said. Vertical is targeting entry into commercial service in 2029. items.title: As If There Was Any Question About Data Centers Being Weak Job Creators, Meta Is Now Deploying Robots to Maintain Them
items.summary: Since the start of the data center boom, “job creation” was one of the key promises made to communities weighing whether to host the tech industry’s monstrous computing facilities in their backyards. That was always a gross over-representation of the facts, as most labor required for data centers comes in the form of temporary construction jobs to build them. Still, the tech tycoons who need data centers to keep the AI revolution chugging along could always fall back on promoting the lonely skeleton crews tasked with manually monitoring, patrolling, and maintaining each facility. Now, even that could be going away. According to new reporting by Ars Technica , the AI giant Meta is testing new robots designed to automate the work of data center maintenance, with the aim of keeping the cost of labor even lower. The initiative is in its very early stages, per Ars , involving trial runs of hardware from a few different robotics firms. These include companies like ABB, Kinova, and Watney Robotics, which supply robot arms being tested for tasks like hot-swapping network cables and cycling power to server racks. One anonymous Meta staffer told Ars that, if it’s successful, a robotic arm from Kinova could replace up to 80 percent of their the facilities’ workload. “We thought those of us performing the physical tasks were safe for a while, but not anymore,” the worker lamented. “It’s coming for us all, unfortunately.” The bulk of data center overhead comes from the hardware itself, particularly the extremely pricey AI chips needed to run high-powered large language models. Even when factoring in construction the human labor cost of data centers is negligible, meaning Meta is going far out of its way to automate maintenance work. Approached for comment by Ars , a Meta spokesperson declined to comment on the testing of robots for data center work. items.title: SAP has a message for software doomsayers: The pendulum will swing back
items.summary: Jan Gilg, SAP's global president of customer success and Americas. SAP A SAP executive anticipates a recovery from the SaaSpocalypse, driven by advances in business AI. SAP is using AI to solidify its competitive edge against Palantir and other tech giants. SAP is shifting more to consumption-based pricing to align AI costs with business outcomes. A SAP executive says the "pendulum will swing back" from the SaaSpocalypse. Like many software companies, the German software giant has seen its stock hit hard over the past year amid competition from AI tools. This stock sell-off of software-as-a-service (SaaS) companies, known as the SaaSpocalypse , has hit companies like Salesforce, SAP, and Workday as Anthropic and OpenAI have introduced tools that could threaten their businesses. SAP's stock has been down about 20% over the past year, though it's been on an upward trend over the past month. When SAP reported its earnings in late July, investors responded positively to the company's cloud-led growth and advances in its business AI. Jan Gilg, SAP's global president of customer success and Americas, told Business Insider that the sell-off was "a bit of an overreaction on the entire industry." "As usual, I feel the pendulum will swing back," Gilg said. "There will be users. There will be losers and winners. I truly believe SAP will be on the side of the winners." To get on the winning side, Gilg says SAP has been reinventing itself with AI, investing in its data capabilities, and changing its pricing models. "Everybody has AI on the agenda right now," Gilg said. SAP bounces back from the SaaSpocalypse SAP's stock has jumped roughly 40% since it reported earnings in late July. There's a reason for that, Gilg says. SAP isn't easily replaceable through a vibe-coded tool , though Gilg does expect companies to leverage AI to build software much faster. Internally, SAP has also used AI to improve its output and build its own software, and it sees AI as an opportunity to improve its tools for customers. "It's really multifaceted. items.title: How to automate your Gmail inbox — without AI
items.summary: Gmail is filled with hidden features and add-on possibilities , but one of the service’s most powerful organizational tools is sitting right in the heart of its regular settings. As you may have guessed by now (especially if you read this story’s headline, you clever little cat), I’m talking about filters — Gmail’s long-standing system for automating your inbox with a series of custom-crafted rules. At a glance, filters can seem complicated. They can seem overwhelming. They can even seem unnecessary. But don’t let yourself be fooled by the feature’s curiously crusty exterior. Gmail filters have the potential to completely reshape your inbox and the way your incoming messages are handled. They can help you keep your email in order with no ongoing thought or effort. And, unlike Google’s new AI Inbox option (which notably still doesn’t seem to be available for most people as of this writing), filters (a) don’t require your personal messages to be processed by generative AI systems — and (b) give you complete control over exactly how your email is handled instead of forcing you to rely on inherently unreliable technology to figure out what you want for you (and then likely come up short at least some of the time). Best of all? All it takes is a teensy touch of one-time planning to get Gmail filters set up to your exact specifications and working for you quietly and automatically from that moment onward. Follow the filter-centric Gmail tips in this guide, and your inbox will be running like a well-oiled (but not too greasy) machine in no time. Part 1: Figuring out your Gmail filters Let’s start by thinking through some Gmail filter possibilities to get an idea for the sorts of setups you might want to consider — then, we’ll go step by step through the process of creating them. With Gmail filters, you could: Ensure messages from specific high-priority senders always go into your inbox’s Primary tab, where you’re certain to see them Ensure specific sorts of lower-priority messages — like invoices, reports, or updates from different services you use — automatically get sorted into an out-of-the-way location and never even show up in your inbox Keep messages from annoying people out of your hair (but still available in case you need to find them) by automatically archiving them as soon as they arrive Forward messages from a specific address or with a specific phrase in their subjects to other members of your team or family Instantly respond to messages to or from a specific address with a prewritten template Label messages sent to a specific variation of your Gmail address (like youraddress+vip@gmail.com) or written with a specific word or phrase in the subject (like “urgent,” “important,” or “hey jerkwad, pay attention to this”) as “VIP” and then receive notifications only for messages with that designation Mark specific types of messages from yourself as reminders by giving them a bright yellow “REMINDER” label that makes them stand out in your inbox Get a snickerdoodle delivered to your desk every time your boss emails you All right, so that last one isn’t really possible (not yet, anyway) — just wanted to make sure you were still paying attention. Everything else in that list, however, is absolutely doable and actually quite easy to set up with Gmail filters. Got some ideas of your own? Good deal. Time to make ’em happen. Part 2: Creating your Gmail filters The simplest way to start a new Gmail filter is to click the control panel icon — the symbol showing three horizontal lines stacked on top of each other — within the big search box at the top of the Gmail website. (Filters can’t easily be managed on mobile, unfortunately, so you’ll need to do all of this in a desktop browser.) That’ll pull up a form where you can fill in whatever you want to use as the basis for your filtering — a word or phase that might appear within an email’s subject or body, an address from which a message could originate, or any other variable or combination of variables you like. The form for creating a filter is filled with options for controlling email automation. JR Raphael / Foundry Fill in the fields as appropriate, using however many variables you want — even employing quotation marks around multiword terms along with operators like “AND” and “OR” between terms, if you really want to get fancy — and then click “Create filter” at the bottom of the box. You can use any combination of variables, even employing operators within a single field, to control when your filter will run. JR Raphael / Foundry One quick warning: By default, your filter will apply to any and all incoming messages — hence the “All Mail” setting that shows up next to the “Search” option in the filter creation pop-up. If you change that option to “Inbox,” you’re likely to see an error message informing you that the parameters you chose are not recommended and may not work properly. Leave that “Search” option set to “All Mail” — which is probably what you want, anyway — and you’ll steer clear of any errors and allow things to work the way they should. Now it’s time for the fun part — the part where you decide exactly what happens when a message meeting your conditions arrives. You can select any combination of actions from the list and then configure them as needed. You can even tell Gmail to apply your filter retroactively to messages already in your account (as opposed to using it only for new messages that arrive from that point forward) by checking the “Also apply filter to matching conversations” option at the bottom of the box. Gmail’s filters include a variety of actions that can execute when your conditions are met. JR Raphael / Foundry Once you’ve got that finished, click the blue “Create filter” button — and that’s it: Your new Gmail filter is officially in place and active. The next time any message comes in that meets the parameters you outlined, the actions you specified will automatically take place faster than you can say “I embrace Workspace in my workplace cyberspace.” Part 3: Managing your Gmail filters Last but not least, make yourself a mental note in case you ever need to adjust your filters in the future: If you want to edit, delete, or even just revisit a filter you created, just click the gear-shaped icon in the upper-right corner of the Gmail website, click “Settings,” then click the “Filters and Blocked Addresses” tab at the top of the settings screen. You’ll see every filter you’ve ever created there and can tweak or remove any of ’em with a couple quick clicks. Now if only we could find a way to get the filters to deliver those blasted snickerdoodles for us. Hey, Google: Any chance you can make that happen? This article was originally published in October 2019 and most recently updated in September 2026.

items.title: Walmart's copycat strategy: Restaurant delivery is its latest use of heft to break into established markets
items.summary: Walmart's main business is still its stores, but the company is always trying new things too. Bloomberg/Getty Images Walmart's move into restaurant delivery is another expansion from selling general merchandise. Since Sam Walton, the retail giant has placed big bets on new lines of business inspired by others. Here's a look back at some of the strategies that worked well for Walmart — and a few that didn't. Walmart got its start in 1962 selling general merchandise as a discount store in Rogers, Arkansas. Founder Sam Walton was constantly on the lookout for new retail concepts to try, and he wasn't shy about borrowing ideas from other successful entrepreneurs. "He just tried things, and he would learn, and if it didn't work, it wasn't a failure," CEO John Furner said during a conversation with reporters at Walmart's headquarters in June. "We just learned from it." Last week, Walmart moved to grow its delivery service in a partnership with Dunkin', putting the company on a collision course with delivery services like DoorDash and Uber Eats. The retailer will eventually offer delivery from most of the 10,000 Dunkin' locations across the US, moving onto turf long dominated by DoorDash and Uber Eats. Walmart described itself as "a rapidly emerging contender in the restaurant delivery business." That delivery experiment is a continuation of a pattern that Furner says is part of Walmart's DNA. "We constantly want to learn. We see where the world's going. Some things apply, some things don't," he said. "We'll learn from it and figure out the best way that we can accelerate the business." Here are eight bets Walmart has placed over the years in its bid to grow beyond traditional discount retailing. Home improvement Eric Thayer / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images One of Walmart's first attempts at branching out came in 1975 with the launch of the Sav-Co Home Improvement Center chain. The brand didn't take off, and Walmart shifted its focus to adding new features to its stores. While local hardware stores were common in this era, large-store formats were relatively uncommon. Home Depot didn't open its first stores until 1979. Pharmacy John Gress/Corbis via Getty Images One of Walmart's early in-store experiments was in the pharmacy business, which began in 1978 and has since grown into one of the company's key business lines. Walmart dispensed an estimated $36.8 billion in prescriptions last year, making it the fifth largest pharmacy in the US, according to the Drug Channels Institute, which tracks the pharmaceutical industry. More recently, Walmart has stepped up prescription delivery speeds, with some orders filled in 30 minutes or less . Auto service Dominick Reuter/Business Insider Walmart opened its first auto care center in Oklahoma in 1979 and the service has expanded to nearly 2,600 locations across the US. Walmart's auto centers have also served as a testing ground for the company's expanding third-party marketplace, with customers able to order products like tires online that are shipped to a local store for scheduled installation. Warehouse club Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images The 80's were a busy decade for Walmart and Sam Walton in terms of experimentation. "'82, '83 I think he opened four different formats in that two year period," Furner said in June. "Sam's Club came out of it and was really successful, and the others we decided not to go forward with." Walton's approach to the wholesale club was modeled on Saul Price's concepts FedMart and Price Club, the latter of which also inspired and eventually merged with Costco. Sam's Club now has more than 600 US locations with $90 billion in sales last year. Grocery Scott Olson/Getty Images The Walmart supercenter is a quintessentially American phenomenon, but Walton famously modeled the concept off the European hypermarket format, which combined general merchandise retail with groceries under a single roof. "It took probably five or six years until there was a store in Washington, Missouri, that worked," Furner said of Walton's attempts to adapt the hypermarket concept to the US. It still took Walmart opening about a dozen more supercenters for the idea to really gain traction, he added. There are now more than 3,500 supercenters and more than 650 neighborhood market grocery stores in the US. Walmart is the largest grocery chain in the country, pulling in roughly one in five dollars spent in the category, according to consumer analytics firm Numerator. Specialty retail Stephen Zenner/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images About a decade ago, Walmart embarked on a flurry of merger activity, snapping up specialty retailers Bonobos, Moosejaw, and Modcloth in a bid to expand the company's reach with specialty brands and e-commerce customers. All three chains remained independent of Walmart's core operations and were subsequently sold off to other owners as the company refocused on its own offerings. Advertising Katie Jones/Variety via Getty Images In 2019, Walmart brought its advertising business in-house with what would become Walmart Connect, which sells ad space for the company's physical and digital properties. Combined with a growing third-party e-commerce marketplace and the acquisition of TV-maker Vizio, Walmart's ads business has delivered significant revenue growth in recent years. Restaurant delivery Walmart Walmart's latest bet puts the company on a course to compete more directly with food delivery apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats. After letting grocery-delivery customers add meals from in-store Subway shops , Walmart said in September it would bring thousands of off-site Dunkin' locations to the service. Walmart has already established itself as a powerhouse in fast delivery for merchandise, groceries, and medicine — now it's set to fulfill more of what other chains sell too. The Walmart supercenter is a quintessentially American phenomenon, but Walton famously modeled the concept off the European hypermarket format, which combined general merchandise retail with groceries under a single roof.

"It took probably five or six years until there was a store in Washington, Missouri, that worked," Furner said of Walton's attempts to adapt the hypermarket concept to the US.

It still took Walmart opening about a dozen more supercenters for the idea to really gain traction, he added.

There are now more than 3,500 supercenters and more than 650 neighborhood market grocery stores in the US. Walmart is the largest grocery chain in the country, pulling in roughly one in five dollars spent in the category, according to consumer analytics firm Numerator.

Specialty retail

Stephen Zenner/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images

About a decade ago, Walmart embarked on a flurry of merger activity, snapping up specialty retailers Bonobos, Moosejaw, and Modcloth in a bid to expand the company's reach with specialty brands and e-commerce customers.

All three chains remained independent of Walmart's core operations and were subsequently sold off to other owners as the company refocused on its own offerings.

Advertising

Katie Jones/Variety via Getty Images

In 2019, Walmart brought its advertising business in-house with what would become Walmart Connect, which sells ad space for the company's physical and digital properties.

Combined with a growing third-party e-commerce marketplace and the acquisition of TV-maker Vizio, Walmart's ads business has delivered significant revenue growth in recent years.

Restaurant delivery

Walmart

Walmart's latest bet puts the company on a course to compete more directly with food delivery apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats.

After letting grocery-delivery customers add meals from in-store Subway shops, Walmart said in September it would bring thousands of off-site Dunkin' locations to the service.

Walmart has already established itself as a powerhouse in fast delivery for merchandise, groceries, and medicine — now it's set to fulfill more of what other chains sell too.

items.title: He waited nearly 20 years to start a company. Now he's the cofounder of a double unicorn.
items.summary: Snehal Antani became a cofounder in his late 30s. His AI hacking startup, Horizon3, now has a market value above $2 billion. Courtesy of Horizon3 Horizon3 CEO Snehal Antani spent two decades building the skills he believed he'd need to be a founder. Antani said that experience helped the startup survive a funding crunch and the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank. There was one skill, though, he hadn't learned and got a crash course in: fundraising. Earlier this month, the AI hacking startup Horizon3 achieved a rare milestone: a $250 million funding round pushed its market valuation above $2 billion, making it a so-called double unicorn. CEO Snehal Antani said he spent nearly two decades acquiring the skills he needed to build the business, which simulates cyberattacks on companies' systems to identify vulnerabilities before real hackers can exploit them. The knowledge he gained turned out to be crucial, first when the tech funding market tightened and, later, when the bank where Horizon3 held all its money collapsed. "I wanted to make sure I built the right experiences," Antani, now 46, told Business Insider. After graduating from college, he said he learned about launching products at IBM, organizational management at GE Capital, scaling a hypergrowth company at software maker Splunk, and leadership at the US Joint Special Operations Command, or JSOC. It was also at JSOC where Antani met Air Force veteran Anthony Pillitiere, his Horizon3 cofounder. A different path Antani's path runs counter to the familiar Silicon Valley image of the college-dropout founder, embodied by figures like Mark Zuckerberg and Bill Gates , who started Facebook and Microsoft, respectively, as teenagers. Yet research suggests successful founders are often older than startup-culture stereotypes imply. An MIT Sloan study published in 2020 analyzed 2.7 million US entrepreneurs and found that the average age of founders behind the fastest-growing 0.1% of new ventures was 45. For Antani, the value of a later start was quickly put to the test. Three years after he founded Horizon3 in 2019, the tech funding environment abruptly changed, and the company suddenly had to make the cash it had raised last much longer than planned. Antani said he recalled a lesson from the CEO of one of his former employers about how to weather an economic downturn: Rather than cut your way through it, sell your way through it. He said Horizon3 did both. The company found about $3 million in costs to cut or redirect, including changes to benefits, hiring plans, and other operating expenses. Then it reinvested that money in sales and marketing, which Antani said helped grow revenue nearly fivefold year over year. Flirting with disaster In 2023, Horizon3 came closer to disaster. As Silicon Valley Bank was collapsing , Antani said he got a text from an investor asking how much of the startup's money was held there. His answer: "100%." By the time federal regulators took it over, Horizon3 had opened an account at another bank. But its funds in Silicon Valley Bank were frozen, and missing payroll could have triggered about $750,000 a day in California penalties — enough, Antani said, to put the company out of business within a week. To prevent that from happening, Antani said he drew $1 million from a personal line of credit. He and his executive team then agreed to tell employees what was happening and what they were doing about it. After regulators restored access to Horizon3's Silicon Valley Bank funds, the company repaid Antani. He said the episode put to use the leadership lessons he learned at JSOC, particularly the importance of dealing with crises. "It's all about being steady, calm, controlled," he said. "You can't be panicked." One learning curve For all the experience Antani brought to Horizon3, there was one part of the founder's job he had never done before: fundraising. To overcome that gap, he said he treated his early investor meetings as a crash course, repeatedly refining his pitch deck, financial model, and market case in response to the questions he was asked. "The first time, you kind of suck," said Antani. "You have to invest in being a good storyteller." After dozens of investor meetings, Antani said he mastered his pitch and received two term sheets , one of which he chose for Horizon3's $3.5 million seed round — the venture-capital firm SignalFire. (The company's latest raise was co-led by NightDragon and NEA.) Today, Horizon3 is far larger than the small team Antani started with, made up of former intelligence, special operations, and enterprise software veterans — mostly people he knew through his past work. The company, one of the earliest companies to bring the concept of an AI hacker to market, has about 7,000 customers globally and 550 employees. Antani said the experience he gained across different companies, roles, and environments made that possible. "You don't want to learn how to deal with HR issues for the first time as a founder," he said. "You want to have learned that stuff ahead of time." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Erin Piacenti, killed in Times Square stabbing, was a 'superstar' at Bank of America known for mentoring junior teammates
items.summary: Erin Piacenti was known for mentoring younger employees. Bank of America Erin Piacenti, who was killed in Times Square on Monday, was known as a mentor at Bank of America. Colleagues remembered her not only for her sharp legal mind, but love of books, Disney, and family. Piacenti's boss remembers describing her as a 'superstar' to senior management before her death. When Erin Piacenti walked into Bank of America on Monday after five months on maternity leave, she found pink daisies sitting on her desk. Welcome signs were strung around the office she shared with a few teammates. Piacenti showed them photos of Madison, her newborn daughter, before settling in to read case law. That afternoon, Piacenti was fatally stabbed in Times Square in what police described as an unprovoked attack. She was 32. Though Piacenti only started as a vice president in the firm's Americas Business Selection and Conflicts group around 18 months ago, she'd already made an impact on the small team. Hallie Ziesmer, the head of the roughly 20-person group, described Piacenti as a "superstar" in conversations with senior management before her death, and remembers interviewing Piacenti at the end of 2024. "It was probably one of the shortest interviews, because I think within three minutes I wanted to hire her," Ziesmer, who was Piacenti's direct boss, said on Friday. "She was obviously very intelligent, very capable. She was polished but down-to-earth." Piacenti was attacked by Pamela Cisneros, 49, who also injured another victim before officers shot her and killed her at the scene. There's been a wave of support on and beyond Wall Street since the event, and a GoFundMe to help her daughter has raised more than $800,000. Many Bank of America employees have contributed, a spokesperson for the bank said. Before joining Bank of America, Piacenti worked at the law firm Davis Polk for more than three years, focusing on mergers and acquisitions for part of that time. She started her career as a buyer at Bloomingdale's and graduated magna cum laude from Fordham Law. Piacenti had a niche focus at the bank, helping investment bankers prepare disclosure documents for companies gearing up for an M&A transaction and clients navigate a thicket of regulations. A colleague remembers her as resourceful, always finding creative solutions on her own. Piacenti would mentor more junior teammates who didn't have the same legal expertise, Ziesmer said. Many of them have spent time in Ziesmer's office this week, remembering how detailed and caring Piacenti was with her help. One junior employee who sat across from Piacenti said in an email that she reviewed much of their work, and had offered personal advice on top of professional tips during their occasional coffees. "She could have, on some days, left the office to be home, but she would spend time with juniors. She wanted them to understand and share a passion for what she was doing. She really enjoyed it," Ziesmer said. Piacenti would often talk about visiting her four younger siblings, or books, or Disney. When the team attended a cooking class last year, the same colleague who admired Piacenti's resourcefulness said she made the best dish (and helped save them, an inadequate chef). When another colleague ran into her on the Q train one morning, she was thrilled to introduce them to her husband, Frank, whom she talked about all the time. Around the holidays, Piacenti brought dozens of cookies into the office after she and Frank hosted the family's Christmas cookie party at their new home in New Jersey. Ziesmer says the team now plans to bring in cookies every year. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Toyota spent years moving slowly on EVs. I drove its new, affordable C-HR to see whether the wait paid off.
items.summary: Toyota took its time developing EVs. Was the C-HR worth the wait? Ben Shimkus/Business Insider Toyota wasn't a big player in the early-2020s all-electric game. It only launched one EV: the bZ4X. Suddenly, there's an influx of Toyota EVs for 2026, when competitors are leaving the market. I drove a new entrant to see if it works — and I think I'm in love. Let's go back to 2023. GM is rolling out a dozen EVs , Ford has borrowed the iconic F-150 and Mustang nameplates for all-electric vehicles, Polestar looks like a potential up-and-comer… And Toyota — long heralded as one of the more environmentally conscious automakers after the runaway success of the Prius hybrid — isn't really competing. Its single EV, the bZ4X, is a little weird-looking, charges slowly, and won't reach 300 miles on a full battery. Toyota's slow approach surprised industry watchers. Environmentalists blew up my phone at the time, complaining that the world's largest automaker was leaning heavily on hybrids that still got most of their power by burning dinosaur juice. Fast-forward three years. The industry's rosier EV predictions have succumbed to billion-dollar write-downs , a big graveyard of discontinued models , and Polestar's removal from the US market. Simultaneously, and almost inexplicably, Toyota's consumer EV lineup in 2026, fresh off a partnership with Subaru, has more nameplates than Tesla. That reversal is what made me particularly curious about the new C-HR. Handsome. Efficient. Kinda… super sporty? The C-HR is more of a looker than its bigger sibling. Ben Shimkus/Business Insider I drove about 200 miles through New York City traffic and New Jersey's highways in a 2026 Toyota C-HR XSE. And man, oh man, did I like my time in the driver's seat. Let's start with pricing. Starting at $37,080, the C-HR isn't Toyota's most affordable EV — that distinction goes to the bigger, $34,980 bZ . The C-HR is, however, the cheapest way to get into an all-wheel-drive Toyota EV. AWD comes standard on the base $37,080 C-HR, while it's a $5,000 upgrade on the bZ. My tester, with two-tone exterior paint, oomph-ier speakers, and some other goodies, topped out at $43,429. The car was wildly efficient. The EPA says the XSE can squeeze 273 miles from a full battery. I would have easily outperformed that during my week. I grabbed the EV with its battery at 89%, and after driving about 170 miles without charging, it never dropped below 40%. That suggests I would have gotten around 400 miles on a charge. On several drives, the car reported efficiency in the high-5s and low-6s in miles per kilowatt-hour. Those numbers, if true and consistent, are phenomenal. It reminded me of my time in Lucid's cars , a high-end EV maker practically obsessed with engineering every possible mile from a battery. The C-HR's interior was comfy and airy. Its storage was a little cramped, though. Ben Shimkus/Business Insider Efficient is not a synonym for boring, and the C-HR makes that super clear. Toyota says the car can jump from a standing start to 60 mph in 4.9 seconds, which would make it the third-quickest car in Toyota's lineup, matching the time of the sport-oriented GR Corolla. Once it merged onto the highway, though, it acted more Toyota-like: composed, comfortable, and whisper-quiet. A Tesla Model Y owner joined me for about two hours, riding mostly in the back seat. They entered the C-HR deeply skeptical that an EV from a legacy automaker could hold a candle to their Tesla — and also walked away impressed with the airy interior and back-seat comfort. Lastly, aesthetics. I think the C-HR looks like it's about to pounce, even when parked. Its smoothed-out edges make it easier on the eyes than Toyota's larger bZ, without falling into the look-at-me-I'm-a-weird-EV styling trap that has befallen plenty of battery-powered cars. The C-HR's curved roofline makes it look like it's about to pounce. It's also a headache for tall backseat passengers. Ben Shimkus/Business Insider My demerits list was small, though potentially substantial for some buyers. There's no glovebox, cramping front-seat storage. My Model Y-owning passenger is about 5-foot-8 and had plenty of headroom in the back, but anyone who regularly lugs tall adults around may have to do some cramming. The trunk is smaller than the bZ's, there's no frunk, and the infotainment occasionally lagged while the car booted up. Still, by the end of the week, I did something I've rarely done after reviewing around 75 cars in my career: I imagined my own life with the C-HR. I was genuinely sad to see the car go. That's not common. Was it worth the wait? Toyota's C-HR smooths the jagged edges found in other modern EVs. Ben Shimkus/Business Insider Showing up late did have advantages. The biggest is charging: The C-HR comes standard with a NACS charging port, the widely accepted charging standard developed by Tesla. That lets Toyota skip some of the awkward charging port transitions other automakers have had to navigate. It also helps Toyota avoid some of the costly EV bets that led rivals to their billion-dollar write-downs. The C-HR, like all of Toyota's other EVs, was jointly developed with Subaru, allowing the companies to share development costs in a period of auto industry decluttering . Most of what makes the C-HR so good feels very Toyota: strong efficiency, a comfortable ride, solid initial quality, and an easy-to-live-with interior. Those are not new competencies for the company. The wait paid off with a great EV. Did Toyota need to wait this long to build it? Maybe not. I'm still glad we got here. Read the original article on Business Insider

Toyota took its time developing EVs. Was the C-HR worth the wait?

Ben Shimkus/Business Insider

  • Toyota wasn't a big player in the early-2020s all-electric game. It only launched one EV: the bZ4X.
  • Suddenly, there's an influx of Toyota EVs for 2026, when competitors are leaving the market.
  • I drove a new entrant to see if it works — and I think I'm in love.

Let's go back to 2023. GM is rolling out a dozen EVs, Ford has borrowed the iconic F-150 and Mustang nameplates for all-electric vehicles, Polestar looks like a potential up-and-comer…

And Toyota — long heralded as one of the more environmentally conscious automakers after the runaway success of the Prius hybrid — isn't really competing. Its single EV, the bZ4X, is a little weird-looking, charges slowly, and won't reach 300 miles on a full battery.

Toyota's slow approach surprised industry watchers. Environmentalists blew up my phone at the time, complaining that the world's largest automaker was leaning heavily on hybrids that still got most of their power by burning dinosaur juice.

Fast-forward three years. The industry's rosier EV predictions have succumbed to billion-dollar write-downs, a big graveyard of discontinued models, and Polestar's removal from the US market.

Simultaneously, and almost inexplicably, Toyota's consumer EV lineup in 2026, fresh off a partnership with Subaru, has more nameplates than Tesla.

That reversal is what made me particularly curious about the new C-HR.

Handsome. Efficient. Kinda… super sporty?The C-HR is more of a looker than its bigger sibling.

Ben Shimkus/Business Insider

I drove about 200 miles through New York City traffic and New Jersey's highways in a 2026 Toyota C-HR XSE. And man, oh man, did I like my time in the driver's seat.

Let's start with pricing. Starting at $37,080, the C-HR isn't Toyota's most affordable EV — that distinction goes to the bigger, $34,980 bZ.

The C-HR is, however, the cheapest way to get into an all-wheel-drive Toyota EV. AWD comes standard on the base $37,080 C-HR, while it's a $5,000 upgrade on the bZ. My tester, with two-tone exterior paint, oomph-ier speakers, and some other goodies, topped out at $43,429.

The car was wildly efficient. The EPA says the XSE can squeeze 273 miles from a full battery.

I would have easily outperformed that during my week. I grabbed the EV with its battery at 89%, and after driving about 170 miles without charging, it never dropped below 40%. That suggests I would have gotten around 400 miles on a charge.

On several drives, the car reported efficiency in the high-5s and low-6s in miles per kilowatt-hour. Those numbers, if true and consistent, are phenomenal. It reminded me of my time in Lucid's cars, a high-end EV maker practically obsessed with engineering every possible mile from a battery.

The C-HR's interior was comfy and airy. Its storage was a little cramped, though.

Ben Shimkus/Business Insider

Efficient is not a synonym for boring, and the C-HR makes that super clear. Toyota says the car can jump from a standing start to 60 mph in 4.9 seconds, which would make it the third-quickest car in Toyota's lineup, matching the time of the sport-oriented GR Corolla.

Once it merged onto the highway, though, it acted more Toyota-like: composed, comfortable, and whisper-quiet.

A Tesla Model Y owner joined me for about two hours, riding mostly in the back seat.

They entered the C-HR deeply skeptical that an EV from a legacy automaker could hold a candle to their Tesla — and also walked away impressed with the airy interior and back-seat comfort.

Lastly, aesthetics. I think the C-HR looks like it's about to pounce, even when parked. Its smoothed-out edges make it easier on the eyes than Toyota's larger bZ, without falling into the look-at-me-I'm-a-weird-EV styling trap that has befallen plenty of battery-powered cars.

The C-HR's curved roofline makes it look like it's about to pounce. It's also a headache for tall backseat passengers.

Ben Shimkus/Business Insider

My demerits list was small, though potentially substantial for some buyers. There's no glovebox, cramping front-seat storage. My Model Y-owning passenger is about 5-foot-8 and had plenty of headroom in the back, but anyone who regularly lugs tall adults around may have to do some cramming. The trunk is smaller than the bZ's, there's no frunk, and the infotainment occasionally lagged while the car booted up.

Still, by the end of the week, I did something I've rarely done after reviewing around 75 cars in my career: I imagined my own life with the C-HR.

I was genuinely sad to see the car go. That's not common.

Was it worth the wait?Toyota's C-HR smooths the jagged edges found in other modern EVs.

Ben Shimkus/Business Insider

Showing up late did have advantages.

The biggest is charging: The C-HR comes standard with a NACS charging port, the widely accepted charging standard developed by Tesla. That lets Toyota skip some of the awkward charging port transitions other automakers have had to navigate.

It also helps Toyota avoid some of the costly EV bets that led rivals to their billion-dollar write-downs. The C-HR, like all of Toyota's other EVs, was jointly developed with Subaru, allowing the companies to share development costs in a period of auto industry decluttering.

Most of what makes the C-HR so good feels very Toyota: strong efficiency, a comfortable ride, solid initial quality, and an easy-to-live-with interior. Those are not new competencies for the company.

The wait paid off with a great EV.

Did Toyota need to wait this long to build it? Maybe not. I'm still glad we got here.
