items.title: Uber says it can replace car ownership. My used Toyota Yaris proved its point.
items.summary: I bought a used car. It was much more expensive than using Uber or Lyft. Alex Bitter/BI I bought a used car one year ago and compared the costs with using Uber and Lyft. The car was much more expensive, even though I made choices to save money. It shows why Uber says that its service competes with car ownership. No one had ever been this excited about a used Toyota Yaris. That was my thought as my wife and I picked up the keys to the car we found on Facebook Marketplace one morning in August 2025. For the first time in seven years of living in the Washington, DC area, we were car owners. It was also a rebuke of sorts for one of the companies I write about most often. For years, Uber executives have said that the company's gig-worker drivers — and, increasingly, the self-driving cars on its app — compete with car ownership. Uber President Andrew MacDonald told a podcast last month that the rising cost of a new car makes owning one a worse deal than several years ago. And CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said last year that the rise of robotaxis will reduce car ownership over the next two decades, making driving a car yourself look "something like horseback riding." So, did I make a horrible mistake spending just over $6,000 on a used sub-compact car that's effectively the next draft horse? Last month, one year after buying my Yaris, I decided to add up all my expenses and compare them with the previous year, when I was car-free and relied on Uber, Lyft, and public transportation. Your milage my vary. Your own calculation will depend on where you live, the cost of your car, how fast it depreciates, and the current price of gas (or charging, if you drive an EV). My results showed that Uber might have a point. The costs of a Toyota Yaris add up My wife and I decided we wanted a car last summer when we realized that parking at our apartment complex was free. Owning a car never made sense to us in Washington. DC is one of about a dozen US cities with a rapid transit system, and a parking spot can cost up to $300 a month. Plus, wait times for rides on Uber and Lyft are rarely more than a few minutes. Parking is just one of the costs of owning a car these days. The average sticker price of a new car is above $50,000, according to Kelly Blue Book, a Cox Automotive brand that tracks car prices. I bought a used car. It was much more expensive than using Uber or Lyft.

Alex Bitter/BI

  • I bought a used car one year ago and compared the costs with using Uber and Lyft.
  • The car was much more expensive, even though I made choices to save money.
  • It shows why Uber says that its service competes with car ownership.

No one had ever been this excited about a used Toyota Yaris.

That was my thought as my wife and I picked up the keys to the car we found on Facebook Marketplace one morning in August 2025. For the first time in seven years of living in the Washington, DC area, we were car owners.

It was also a rebuke of sorts for one of the companies I write about most often. For years, Uber executives have said that the company's gig-worker drivers — and, increasingly, the self-driving cars on its app — compete with car ownership.

Uber President Andrew MacDonald told a podcast last month that the rising cost of a new car makes owning one a worse deal than several years ago. And CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said last year that the rise of robotaxis will reduce car ownership over the next two decades, making driving a car yourself look "something like horseback riding."

So, did I make a horrible mistake spending just over $6,000 on a used sub-compact car that's effectively the next draft horse?

Last month, one year after buying my Yaris, I decided to add up all my expenses and compare them with the previous year, when I was car-free and relied on Uber, Lyft, and public transportation.

Your milage my vary. Your own calculation will depend on where you live, the cost of your car, how fast it depreciates, and the current price of gas (or charging, if you drive an EV).

My results showed that Uber might have a point.

The costs of a Toyota Yaris add up

My wife and I decided we wanted a car last summer when we realized that parking at our apartment complex was free.

Owning a car never made sense to us in Washington. DC is one of about a dozen US cities with a rapid transit system, and a parking spot can cost up to $300 a month. Plus, wait times for rides on Uber and Lyft are rarely more than a few minutes.

Parking is just one of the costs of owning a car these days. The average sticker price of a new car is above $50,000, according to Kelly Blue Book, a Cox Automotive brand that tracks car prices. Used cars, while more affordable, have become more expensive, too. There's also maintenance, insurance, and, for many of us, the elevated price of gas.

When my wife and I found our used Toyota Yaris L — that's "L" meaning the lowest-trim model — we thought that we were being as thrifty as possible. We could buy the car without a loan. And my research suggested that, even when it needed repairs, they wouldn't be that expensive on a small, simple vehicle. If any car had a chance of rivaling the cost of Uber, this was it.

But it didn't.

After buying the car for $6,000, one year of car ownership cost us another $5,000.

That's more than three times as much as the $1,600 we spent on ride-hailing trips and rental cars in the year before we bought the car.

Some of the expenses were optional, like $250 to have my transmission fluid drained and replaced as a preventative maintenance measure. But most of those costs were the basics: Oil changes, gas, registration fees, insurance, and tolls.

I also didn't quit using Uber or Lyft. I took rides to plenty of weekend bar hangs with friends, either because parking was a hassle or because I wanted to drink.

Suddenly, free parking started to lose its shine. Our little sub-compact was more expensive than I had expected.

Maybe, though, there's more to it.

'Ready to be driven at a moment's notice'

I'm merely the latest person to compare whether owning a car makes sense in the era of ride-hailing apps. Even Sam Altman made the comparison in a blog post back in 2014.

His conclusion: Using Uber was cheaper than driving his Tesla Roadster — at least, back when the millennial life subsidy made fares on the app cheaper than they are today.

Doing a strict cost comparison isn't how most of us think about car ownership, though, according to David Keith, associate professor of strategy at the Melbourne Business School in Australia.

Keith is one of the authors of a 2021 study that asked drivers from major US cities how much they would need to be paid annually to give up their car.

The exact number — $11,197 on average — wasn't as interesting as why people said that they valued owning a car. More than half of that amount, Keith and colleagues found, was "non-use value," which includes having the option to take a car whenever you want, and a perceived status boost from owning a car.

In other words, drivers are okay if their car sits unused most of the time. "I can walk outside, and there's this box of metal sitting there on the street, ready to be driven at a moment's notice," he said.

I knew exactly what he meant.

For weeks after buying my car, I had to change how I thought about transportation. Questions like "How much are Uber rides?" and "Is my destination accessible by Metro?" were replaced by a single statement: "Just drive there now, stupid!"

There were also places I would never have visited without a car: For example, Fredericksburg, Virginia, for a day of antiquing, or rural Maryland to search the site of a Civil War camp with my metal detector. Being able to hop in a car whenever you want feels great. Those are trips that would have been difficult or impossible with Uber, and they're the main reason that my wife and I plan to keep our car, extra costs and all.

Recreating that freedom with modes of transportation that you don't own is an important aspect of reducing car ownership in the US, Keith told me.

Some places have tried it. A company called MaaS Global — that's "Mobility as a service" — operated an app called Whim, which offered taxi rides, bike shares, and public transit as a bundle for a monthly subscription. Whim operated in several European cities, including Helsinki and Vienna, before MaaS Global filed for bankruptcy in 2024 and ceased operations.

Meanwhile, in the US, car ownership has stayed steady over the last couple of decades, even as alternatives from Uber and Lyft to local bike-sharing programs grow.

"All of these things are fantastic, but none of them have really led to there being fewer cars in cities," Keith said.

items.title: One runner spent $40,000, another took a second job. Marathoners are making big sacrifices to chase medals worldwide.
items.summary: David Boyce, who takes runcations, competing in the London Marathon in 2024. Courtesy of David Boyce When some people travel, they collect fridge magnets or shot glasses. Eugen Godun collects marathon medals. Last March, the 34-year-old software developer earned the coveted Six Star medal for running the Boston, Chicago, New York City , London, Berlin, and Tokyo marathons, known as the original World Marathon Majors. When Godun crossed the finish line in Japan, he burst into tears, overcome by a mixture of pride, happiness, and pure exhaustion. Godun started running in 2014 and completed his first international marathon in Poland the following year, shaving an hour off his previous time of 4 hours and 6 minutes. Over the past decade, his pursuit of medals and faster finishes has taken him from his home in Kyiv to eight countries across Europe, the US, and Asia. For amateur runners like Godun, destination races kill several birds with one stone: a trip abroad, a major athletic achievement , and some serious bragging rights. Godun is particularly proud to be one of only 60 Ukrainians recorded as having received a Six Star medal. For all their rewards, international marathons demand plenty in return: vacation days, family time, and money. In 11 years, Godun said he has spent roughly $40,000 on international marathon trips, or $5,000 a race on average. Godun sometimes wonders where he'd be financially if he'd saved the money instead. "Maybe if I switched these marathons for saving money, I'd be able to buy my own apartment,” he said. Even so, he thinks it was worth it. "I like to spend my money on experiences, not on things," Godun added. Godun received his Six Star medal after running the Tokyo Marathon in 2025. Courtesy of Eugen Godun Have you taken on a second job, gone into debt, or found an unusual way to make the numbers work to pursue a passion? Business Insider wants to hear about the trade-offs you've made for a hobby. Contact this reporter at jzitser@businessinsider.com . The pursuit of far-flung finish lines Running’s pandemic-era boom shows little sign of fading, and Americans are prioritizing fitness and experience-led travel . More than 52.3 million Americans went road-running in 2025, up more than a million from 2024, according to the Outdoor Industry Association's 2026 Running Report, which is based on data from the Physical Activity Council. In KPMG's summer 2026 consumer survey, half of respondents named physical fitness as their top wellness priority, while 54% of those planning to travel more were seeking a specific experience or event. Destination marathons combine the two. Godun has plenty of company in the expensive pursuit of far-flung finish lines. Demand for marathon spots has grown in recent years, with international competitors accounting for an increasing share of participants, according to data shared with Business Insider by five of the now-seven World Marathon Majors, the global series of marathon races. Godun ran the New York City Marathon in 2019. Courtesy of Eugen Godun Since 2023, international applications for the London Marathon have almost tripled, from 89,108 in 2023 to 258,502 in 2026, when the race drew 854,452 applicants overall. The Boston Marathon’s share of international runners has risen from about a quarter of the field in 2023 to roughly a third of the 30,000 participants in each of the past three years. The Sydney Marathon has seen even more dramatic international growth. The number of overseas finishers jumped from 260 in 2022 to more than 13,500 of a total 32,963 runners in 2025, when it became the seventh World Marathon Major. “People like a challenge, particularly one that is tough but achievable, and completing the six, or now seven, race series has become the ultimate running challenge,” Steven Seaton, the founder of the UK-based sports tourism firm 2:09 Events, said. “The fact that the races are hard and increasingly expensive to enter only seems to fuel greater demand.” The cost for international competitors entering the World Marathon Majors ranges from about $237 for Sydney to $333 for New York, before accounting for flights, hotels, food, and other costs. Godun, for example, has tried to cut costs by staying with friends, where possible, and drawn a line on what he’s willing to spend. He gave up a spot in the 2026 Sydney Marathon because he couldn't justify spending thousands of dollars on flights. He said he has since started setting aside about $1,000 a month, or about 20% of his monthly income, to avoid ruling out future races on cost alone. Godun has found himself working harder at his job, too. “I need to earn more money to be able to do this,” he said. A second job to keep chasing marathon medals David Boyce, 59, is so committed to running international marathons that he took on a part-time job lecturing at a local university three years ago to, in his words, “feed my addiction.” The extra income has helped the Canadian government employee pay for a coach, enter races farther afield, and spend longer abroad exploring the destinations. In the lead-up to a marathon, Boyce prioritizes rest, saving the indulgences for later. “Then you can do all the things that you want to do, like have a beer, have a decadent meal, or things like that,” Boyce said. Boyce ran the Boston Marathon in 2022. Courtesy of David Boyce In his early 40s, Boyce couldn’t have imagined organizing his vacations around marathons. Then, 16 years ago, he got a frightening wake-up call when his heart began pounding during an uphill bike ride. A stranger called an ambulance, and he ended up in the hospital. “They put a heart monitor on me and figured out nothing was really wrong,” he said. “I was just really out of shape.” He started with treadmill running, then moved to 10k runs, before completing a local marathon in 2016. Two years later, he traveled to Chicago for his first international runcation. Now, he’s a Five Star finisher, with only Tokyo left to complete the set. His first marathon took him more than four hours. A decade later, as he approaches 60, Boyce is running closer to 3 hours and 30 minutes and is considering pushing himself further with an Ironman or an ultramarathon. “For me, it's the sense of accomplishment,” he said. “The personal goal, to see if I can do it, to push myself to a different limit.” Boyce said the improvements to his health and fitness make the sacrifices, like having a second job, worthwhile. His goal is to keep “beating back the old man.” Using up almost all vacation days As well as money, runcations can eat up another valuable resource: time. Next year, Boyce plans to spend three of his four weeks of vacation in Japan for the Tokyo Marathon. In the past, Godun has devoted as much as 80% of his 20 days of annual leave to runcations. Last year, he used some of the time freed up from earning his Six Star on a two-week beach vacation in Spain. “It's not for me, this type of pleasure,” he said. Every year, Kevin Lock, a 45-year-old bank employee, and his wife, who is also a marathon runner, meticulously map out their four weeks of vacation days on a spreadsheet. They allot their time off between races and other personal travel, prioritizing races held around federal holidays to preserve vacation days. The couple doesn't always race together. Since 2022, Lock has run three marathons, including New York, Chicago, and Boston, as well as 16 half-marathons across the US. His wife, meanwhile, ran the Sydney Marathon without him. Kevin Lock has run marathons in the US, including the New York City marathon. Courtesy of Kevin Lock The couple, based in Charlotte, North Carolina, is equally strategic with money. “I'm fairly crafty at using credit card points ,” Lock said. He generally uses his points for flights to and from races, while his wife uses hers for hotels, helping them “minimize the financial impact” of marathon trips. They draw from a pool of savings, replenish it regularly, and pay off their credit card balances in full each month. “We want to do these things,” Lock said, “but not at the forfeit of going into debt.” Losing out on family time Not every cost can be offset with credit-card points, careful budgeting, or a vacation spreadsheet. For Vincent Hsu, a physician based in Orlando, money isn’t a huge concern. The biggest trade-off has been family time . “I'm trying to balance my wanting to really achieve running goals that I never thought possible with the need to make sure that I am tending to the needs of my family,” he said. Hsu said he tries to train early in the morning while his wife and 15-year-old son are asleep. Even so, the trips away for races and the sheer amount of time he spends training have both become “stressors” at home. His wife sometimes asks, “Oh, you're running again?” “I'm a little bit sheepish about that,” he said. Hsu's marathon hobby has become a source of stress at home, he said. Courtesy of Vincent Hsu Next March, Hsu plans to run the Tokyo Marathon, but he doesn't know whether his wife, who often likes to come along on trips, can join him. They haven't yet found someone they trust to take care of their teenage son. For all the sacrifices, running has contributed to significant weight loss, introduced him to new friends, and given him a sense of accomplishment. It has proved hard to stop, too. “It is addictive,” he said. Hsu said the prestige of joining the Six Star medal club is also part of the motivation. “It's a great goal. It's coveted. It's desired,” he said. “People are jealous. I readily admit that.” For globe-trotting marathon runners, the medals may be priceless. Collecting them is anything but. items.title: I resigned and couldn't find a job. I lived with family, lost my storage unit, and relied on government assistance.
items.summary: Kymberly McClain struggled to find work for nearly two years after resigning from her deputy director role. Kymberly McClain Kymberly McClain struggled to find work for nearly two years after resigning from her nonprofit role. She eventually deleted her LinkedIn account out of frustration and relied on government assistance. McClain shared how she navigated her long job search and eventually found a call center job. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Kymberly McClain, a 45-year-old who lives in Las Vegas. She previously worked at a small nonprofit until resigning in 2024. The following has been edited for length and clarity. Two years ago, I was working as a deputy director at a small nonprofit in California focused on providing resources for the homeless population. After some leadership changes, I didn't feel like I had the support I needed. In August 2024, I resigned. When I started looking for a new job , I was so confident. I'd gained experience and felt like I'd parted ways on good terms, even getting a letter of recommendation. I thought I was going to slide into another role. Instead, I struggled to find work for nearly two years. I started applying for jobs I never expected to consider When I started looking, I was applying for deputy director, program manager, case manager, and other social service roles. I used LinkedIn, Indeed, ZipRecruiter, CareerBuilder, and other job sites. I sought out résumé help because I had been out of the job market for a few years and didn't know what had changed. September, October, November, and December went by, and nothing happened. As the search continued, I started broadening the scope of the types of jobs I was applying for. I went from thinking I could easily land another deputy director job to applying for retail jobs at places like Burlington Coat Factory. I was willing to take anything. Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers in tech and other industries are navigating their careers. Share your story with him by filling out this form , emailing him , or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. Follow his work by clicking here . I eventually deleted LinkedIn out of frustration LinkedIn was probably the platform I used most during the first six months of my search. I went to LinkedIn training sessions about how to get a job and read up on interview tips. At one point, I was applying to multiple jobs a day and changing my résumé for each one. I would research the company and position before applying. But I wasn't having any luck. I remember seeing comments from other people on LinkedIn asking whether anyone else was having trouble finding a job or getting employers to respond. As the rejections piled up, I started questioning everything. Was it my race? My age ? My lack of a college education? I even wondered whether I was on somebody's list of people not to hire. I had never imagined that I would be without a job for this long. After about a year of searching, I was exhausted by the rejection. I started pulling back from my job search and eventually deleted my LinkedIn account out of frustration. I thought, What's the point? My long job search created financial challenges My job search took a toll on my finances, and I had to apply for government assistance . For a while, I went back and forth between staying with a friend in California and with family in Las Vegas while I tried to figure things out. Kymberly McClain struggled to find work for nearly two years after resigning from her deputy director role.

Kymberly McClain

  • Kymberly McClain struggled to find work for nearly two years after resigning from her nonprofit role.
  • She eventually deleted her LinkedIn account out of frustration and relied on government assistance.
  • McClain shared how she navigated her long job search and eventually found a call center job.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Kymberly McClain, a 45-year-old who lives in Las Vegas. She previously worked at a small nonprofit until resigning in 2024. The following has been edited for length and clarity.

Two years ago, I was working as a deputy director at a small nonprofit in California focused on providing resources for the homeless population.

After some leadership changes, I didn't feel like I had the support I needed. In August 2024, I resigned.

When I started looking for a new job, I was so confident. I'd gained experience and felt like I'd parted ways on good terms, even getting a letter of recommendation.

I thought I was going to slide into another role. Instead, I struggled to find work for nearly two years.

I started applying for jobs I never expected to consider

When I started looking, I was applying for deputy director, program manager, case manager, and other social service roles.

I used LinkedIn, Indeed, ZipRecruiter, CareerBuilder, and other job sites. I sought out résumé help because I had been out of the job market for a few years and didn't know what had changed.

September, October, November, and December went by, and nothing happened.

As the search continued, I started broadening the scope of the types of jobs I was applying for. I went from thinking I could easily land another deputy director job to applying for retail jobs at places like Burlington Coat Factory. I was willing to take anything.

Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers in tech and other industries are navigating their careers. Share your story with him by filling out this form, emailing him, or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. Follow his work by clicking here.

I eventually deleted LinkedIn out of frustration

LinkedIn was probably the platform I used most during the first six months of my search.

I went to LinkedIn training sessions about how to get a job and read up on interview tips. At one point, I was applying to multiple jobs a day and changing my résumé for each one. I would research the company and position before applying.

But I wasn't having any luck. I remember seeing comments from other people on LinkedIn asking whether anyone else was having trouble finding a job or getting employers to respond.

As the rejections piled up, I started questioning everything. Was it my race? My age? My lack of a college education? I even wondered whether I was on somebody's list of people not to hire. I had never imagined that I would be without a job for this long.

After about a year of searching, I was exhausted by the rejection. I started pulling back from my job search and eventually deleted my LinkedIn account out of frustration. I thought, What's the point?

My long job search created financial challenges

My job search took a toll on my finances, and I had to apply for government assistance. For a while, I went back and forth between staying with a friend in California and with family in Las Vegas while I tried to figure things out. Eventually, I moved in with my family members in Las Vegas.

Eventually, I felt like I needed to contribute financially to the household. I had to choose between helping my family and paying for the storage unit I'd stored my belongings in when I moved, so I gave up the unit and lost the belongings in it.

When I wasn't looking for work, I focused more of my time on a nonprofit I'd founded years earlier, based partly on my own experiences navigating the social services system. It helps people experiencing homelessness and domestic violence survivors navigate housing and other resources.

It wasn't generating income, but I needed to feel like I was doing something productive.

Sometimes rejection is redirection

Earlier this year, I gave the job market another try. I applied for several healthcare billing roles, but I was rejected from all of them.

Then, my daughter sent me a link to a remote customer-service job. I completed an assessment, went through the process, and got a yes.

It's a full-time customer-service call center job. It pays significantly less than I made in my prior role, but after being out of work for so long, I'm just excited somebody said yes. When I got the offer, I thought, Okay, I'm not blackballed from the job market.

I'm still not sure what the future holds, but I plan to keep working on my nonprofit while I work this new job.

My advice to other job seekers is to have faith in closed doors. Sometimes rejection is redirection, and sometimes it's the push you need to build something of your own.

items.title: Sam Altman says he's 'a mega Apple fan boy' and is sad they are suing OpenAI
items.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman looks past then-Apple CEO Tim Cook during a dinner for tech leaders at the White House in September 2025. Bloomberg/Getty Images OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is a self-described "mega Apple fanboy." Altman said he was "very sad" to see Apple sue OpenAI. The legal fight illustrates how frayed the relationship between the two companies has become. Sam Altman 's love for Apple is being tested by that pesky detail: the Cupertino tech giant's lawsuit against OpenAI. "I'm like a mega Apple fanboy, and I was very sad about that," Altman told tech journalist Alex Heath during a recent interview. In July, Apple sued OpenAI , accusing the ChatGPT creator of a "coordinated pattern of misconduct at an institutional level" to steal Apple's closely held secrets. OpenAI has said it has "no interest in other companies' trade secrets" and that the lawsuit doesn't live up to Apple's "reputation for obsessing over the smallest details." Altman said when he first heard about the suit, he thought something had gone significantly wrong. "When I first heard about it, I was like, 'Man, this sounds egregious. Someone must have done something badly,'" Altman said. "We don't want any company's IP, and we certainly don't want people who are going to take a company's IP and bring it to us." Altman is barely mentioned in Apple's initial 40-page complaint, which, in addition to various corporate entities, directly named only two OpenAI employees, Chang Liu and Tang Tan , both of whom formerly worked for Apple, as defendants. Apple's suit said Liu and Tan took or retained confidential information when they left the company and, in some instances, asked current Apple employees about unannounced products. The lawsuit marks a dramatic turn from what had once been a major partnership. In June 2024, Altman went to Cupertino to announce that Apple would integrate ChatGPT across its products. Their cooperation has frayed as OpenAI has entered the consumer space Apple has long dominated. Less than a year after speaking at Apple's Worldwide Developer Conference, Altman and iPhone designer Jony Ive announced that they had been collaborating for years and that OpenAI would acquire Ive's startup IO for nearly $6.5 billion. As part of the legal battle, Apple requested a preliminary injunction, which could potentially delay OpenAI's plans. In response, OpenAI said Apple is trying to delay OpenAI's hardware "because it fears OpenAI's product might reduce demand for Apple's." The Apple of his eye Altman is seen at the 2024 Apple Worldwide Developers Conference Nic Coury/AFP via Getty Images Altman's love for Apple is well documented. In 2008, he demoed Loopt, the location-based social networking app he cofounded, at Apple's Worldwide Developer Conference. Altman said getting up onstage required Apple CEO Steve Jobs' approval. Looking back on the experience, he called it "a career highlight" and said it was "the only time in business" he felt that much anxiety. "It was like Steve Jobs, you know," Altman said in 2015, recalling how he grew up viewing Jobs as an iconic figure. Altman said growing up, his first computer was a Macintosh LC II . In 2024, he told Bill Gates that he still owns it and it still works. When Altman announced his partnership with Ive, he cited his hope to bring "some of the delight, wonder and creative spirit that I first felt using an Apple Computer 30 years ago." Speaking with Ive and Laurene Powell Jobs last year, Altman declared the iPhone "the crowning achievement of consumer products" during an onstage interview last November. Altman, who does not own a stake in OpenAI, built his fortune largely through investments in companies including Stripe and Reddit. His grandma gave him what may have been one of his first tech investments. In a 2016 interview, he conducted with his brother Jack, the pair recalled how, for their birthdays, their grandma gave them equal shares in companies she thought they would like. Jack was given Applebee's, while Sam received Apple. "I still have those Apple shares marked in my brokerage account as 'Grandma's birthday Apple shares,' Sam Altman said, adding, "I'm going to keep them." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Convicted CEO who fled LA for Germany is now one of FBI's most wanted fraudsters
items.summary: At least $7.3 million of investor money is alleged to have ended up in Bernhard Fritsch's personal accounts  — funding a Rolls-Royce, a yacht, and a mortgage on his Malibu villa. Mike Windle/Getty Images for StarClub Bernhard Fritsch rubbed elbows with stars and owned a McLaren. Now he's a convicted fraudster, a fugitive, and a top target of the FBI. He can't be extradited from Germany, where he fled after cutting his ankle bracelet. On a sunny day in April, visits a hilltop near Lake Starnberg in Germany. After a hike against the backdrop of the Bavarian mountain panorama, he treats himself to a slice of cake with vanilla ice cream at the Forsthaus Ilkahöhe, a popular hikers' inn. Later, he uploads photos of the outing to Instagram, gushing over the view of the snowy Zugspitze mountain. Does someone who is on the run and wanted by the American federal police post something like that? It is, by far, not the only question raised by this bizarre case. A $150,000 bounty, a severed ankle monitor, escape from US authorities, and an arrest in Mexico — the Bernhard Fritsch file reads like a Hollywood script. On Thursday, the FBI added the 65-year-old German to its "Most Wanted Fraudsters" list . Fritsch studied audio engineering in Berlin in the 1980s before moving to New York in the 1990s. With his company MCY, he wanted to sell music over the internet — sort of a precursor to the streaming giant Spotify at an early stage of the dot-com economy. He told a reporter from the German Manager Magazin in 2000 that he had already won over Michael Jackson, Paul McCartney, Luciano Pavarotti, and the Backstreet Boys to his idea. "You wouldn't believe who's already walked through that door," he said at the time. He had met Michael Jackson in Munich the previous year. Michael Jackson and Bernhard Fritsch at a charity event. Peter Bischoff/Getty Images Sometime in the early 2010s, Fritsch relocated from New York to Santa Monica, California, where he founded the company StarClub. Its app, StarSite, was meant to help celebrities and influencers monetize their reach through advertising. Between 2014 and 2017, according to federal officials, Fritsch raised between $20 million and $30 million from investors. To raise that much, Fritsch apparently relied on prominent connections. In California, he was seen as a skilled operator behind the scenes, Los Angeles Magazine reported. While spending time in Germany, the Bavarian had cultivated ties to the world of celebrities, too: Photos show him with three-time Wimbledon-winner Boris Becker — who in 2022 was sentenced to prison in the UK for tax evasion — and in 2016, Fritsch walked the red carpet with actor Wesley Snipes at Bertelsmann's summer party in Berlin. He also courted proximity to show business in the U.S. In 2014, for example, he had actor Tyrese Gibson (best known from the "Fast & Furious" movies) host a private StarClub party for him. Singer Enrique Iglesias was also linked to the project, and actresses Caitlin O'Connor and Elise Neal appeared at promotional events. According to the website Courthouse News, one investor later claimed in a lawsuit that Fritsch owed him $750,000 for arranging contacts with Jessica Simpson. Tyrese Gibson and Bernhard Fritsch attend a StarClub party in 2014. Mike Windle/Getty Images for StarClub In 2017, Fritsch was criminally charged by federal prosecutors who alleged he made false statements to investors about the app, claiming his company would strike deals with major media companies like Disney and that acquisition offers were forthcoming. At least $7.3 million of investor money is alleged to have ended up in his personal accounts instead — funding a McLaren, a Rolls-Royce, a yacht, and a mortgage on his villa near the popular Carbon Beach in Malibu. In April last year, after a nine-day trial, a jury found him guilty on one of two counts of wire fraud, a verdict for which he could have faced up to 20 years in prison. And then, suddenly, Fritsch was gone. In June 2025, according to the FBI, he cut off his court-ordered ankle monitor and fled to Mexico. This is particularly striking given that his attorney, Kirk Schenck, had argued there was no flight risk, since Fritsch would be leaving his two children behind. According to Mexican authorities, the entrepreneur turned up, of all places, in the state of Sinaloa — considered a stronghold of Mexico's powerful drug cartels. An arrest warrant from Los Angeles followed, and American officials alerted Mexican police. In September of last year, Mexican authorities caught him — allegedly carrying forged documents. After his arrest, Mexican police released him on the condition that he check in at the station every two weeks. Authorities say Fritsch used the opportunity to travel to Mexico City, where in early October he boarded a Lufthansa flight to Munich. The FBI believes he has been in Bavaria ever since. In his absence, a federal judge in Los Angeles sentenced him in absentia to 15 years in prison, a $35,000 fine, and nearly $26.8 million in restitution. Fritsch need not fear extradition. Article 16 of Germany's constitutional Law forbids the extradition of German citizens. So as long as he doesn't leave the country, no US arrest warrant can reach him. The FBI put Fritsch on its list of most-wanted fraudsters. FBI Fritsch's partner, former actress Lucy Weist, pleaded guilty in June of this year to being an accessory after the fact, and she now faces up to five years in prison. FBI Director Kash Patel in June launched the "Most Wanted Fraudsters" list as a counterpart to the classic most-wanted list — this one for white-collar criminals. The goal, Patel said, is to hold "the worst of the worst" accountable. Patrick Grandy, the FBI agent leading the investigation in Los Angeles, describes California as especially fertile ground for fraudsters — and has made clear that the hunt for Fritsch continues. The feds have put up a $150,000 bounty. A request for comment sent to Fritsch via his Instagram profile was not answered. Since his post about the mountain walk in April, Fritsch hasn't uploaded anything new to his profile. He does seem to have been indulging in old memories from time to time. He has captioned several posts "Throwback": One, a photo from 1999 showing him with Michael Jackson, another from 2001 showing him shaking hands with Pope John Paul II at the Vatican. items.title: Two scientists made huge bets on 'impossible' cancer treatments. They're finally paying off.
items.summary: Tal Zaks, the former chief medical officer of Moderna, said he took "a very large financial bet just based on first principle beliefs." Mike Coppola/Getty Images for Klick Health 2026 is the year of the cancer breakthrough, with innovations from Revolution Medicines and Moderna. "I'm almost tired of saying paradigm shift, but I haven't figured out a new phrase," one expert said. Innovators Greg Verdine and Tal Zaks pushed boundaries with risky, groundbreaking experiments. Short sellers love to profit from biotech's big fails. The category remains their favorite to bet against because roughly two-thirds of publicly traded biotech companies ultimately go broke one way or another, losing money for investors. This summer, however, that strategy went bust. Biotech has experienced unusual success with some of the category's biggest, longest cancer moonshots coming to fruition. On August 19, Moderna announced positive late-stage results from a melanoma trial, sending its stock surging 177% — up to $174 per share — on the promise of the very first personalized cancer vaccine . A week later, on August 26, another astounding development: The FDA approved a pill to help treat late-stage prostate cancer. The drug is a new molecular "glue" from Revolution Medicines, a Silicon Valley-based biotech company, and it's capable of drugging so-called undruggable cancer targets. "This is a whole new era," Dr. Andrew Coveler, who directs the Fred Hutch Pancreatic Cancer Specialty Clinic in Seattle, said. "I'm almost tired of saying paradigm shift, but I haven't figured out a new phrase." These medicines are both used in concert with existing drugs, and neither is considered a cure for cancer. Instead, they're seen as breakthrough options that open up a new playing field for fighting cancer, targeting different mutations, and training the immune system in new ways. The moves prompted a huge surge of cash for investors in the companies, prompting celebration at corporate offices. "We raised our glass of champagne, but now back to work," Dr. Alan Sandler, the chief development officer at Revolution Medicines, said. The successes weren't always obvious, though. Two innovators — a chemical biologist and an oncologist — had both the vision and the capital to finally make these groundbreaking ideas work, despite many failures before. A chemist who raised $125 million to chase an idea inspired by nature Greg Verdine is a chemical biologist and former Harvard professor turned biotech entrepreneur. He turned to nature for inspiration to design a new molecular "glue" to target cancer. Greg Verdine In 2012, after four years of pleading for cash, Greg Verdine finally scrounged up the investors to give him $125 million for a cancer drug. He didn't have a drug yet. In fact, he wasn't exactly sure how it could be made. He just had an idea inspired by nature for targeting one of cancer's most "undruggable" mutations, RAS. The problem with RAS is that it is so smooth. Unlike other molecules, this protein has no characteristic sticky pockets or holes for a drug to glom onto. "I have much, much less pain than I had four months ago, when I was diagnosed," Sasse told "60 Minutes" in April. "And I have a massive 76% reduction in tumor volume." items.summary_html:
Tal Zaks, the former chief medical officer of Moderna, said he took "a very large financial bet just based on first principle beliefs."

Mike Coppola/Getty Images for Klick Health

  • 2026 is the year of the cancer breakthrough, with innovations from Revolution Medicines and Moderna.
  • "I'm almost tired of saying paradigm shift, but I haven't figured out a new phrase," one expert said.
  • Innovators Greg Verdine and Tal Zaks pushed boundaries with risky, groundbreaking experiments.

Short sellers love to profit from biotech's big fails. The category remains their favorite to bet against because roughly two-thirds of publicly traded biotech companies ultimately go broke one way or another, losing money for investors.

This summer, however, that strategy went bust. Biotech has experienced unusual success with some of the category's biggest, longest cancer moonshots coming to fruition.

On August 19, Moderna announced positive late-stage results from a melanoma trial, sending its stock surging 177% — up to $174 per share — on the promise of the very first personalized cancer vaccine. A week later, on August 26, another astounding development: The FDA approved a pill to help treat late-stage prostate cancer. The drug is a new molecular "glue" from Revolution Medicines, a Silicon Valley-based biotech company, and it's capable of drugging so-called undruggable cancer targets.

"This is a whole new era," Dr. Andrew Coveler, who directs the Fred Hutch Pancreatic Cancer Specialty Clinic in Seattle, said. "I'm almost tired of saying paradigm shift, but I haven't figured out a new phrase."

These medicines are both used in concert with existing drugs, and neither is considered a cure for cancer. Instead, they're seen as breakthrough options that open up a new playing field for fighting cancer, targeting different mutations, and training the immune system in new ways.

The moves prompted a huge surge of cash for investors in the companies, prompting celebration at corporate offices.

"We raised our glass of champagne, but now back to work," Dr. Alan Sandler, the chief development officer at Revolution Medicines, said.

The successes weren't always obvious, though.

Two innovators — a chemical biologist and an oncologist — had both the vision and the capital to finally make these groundbreaking ideas work, despite many failures before.

A chemist who raised $125 million to chase an idea inspired by natureGreg Verdine is a chemical biologist and former Harvard professor turned biotech entrepreneur. He turned to nature for inspiration to design a new molecular "glue" to target cancer.

Greg Verdine

In 2012, after four years of pleading for cash, Greg Verdine finally scrounged up the investors to give him $125 million for a cancer drug.

He didn't have a drug yet. In fact, he wasn't exactly sure how it could be made. He just had an idea inspired by nature for targeting one of cancer's most "undruggable" mutations, RAS.

The problem with RAS is that it is so smooth. Unlike other molecules, this protein has no characteristic sticky pockets or holes for a drug to glom onto. Even if you could figure out how to attach something to the smooth surface of this protein, you'd run the risk of having your therapy stick onto everything else in the body, too, potentially damaging healthy organs.

"People told me it was crazy. It'll never work"- Greg Verdine

This is why most chemists before him gave up and called RAS an impossible mutation to target, even though it often drives tumor growth in some very tough-to-treat cancers, including pancreatic cancer, colon cancer, and lung cancer.

"I just found it totally unacceptable, pathetic, that we would say, 'Oh, well!' You've got all these patients," Verdine said. "We know exactly what's driving their cancer, but 'Oh, that's undruggable.' Come on!"

Verdine knew that molecular glues already existed in the natural world. Compounds produced by bacteria and fungi cause proteins to bind together, altering their function without completely destroying them. Some immunosuppressive drugs for organ transplantation take advantage of that biology.

The remaining question was: How can you engineer a new way to do that, targeting the "undruggable" RAS cancer mutation? By sticking the drug to another target, then gluing it onto RAS.

"People told me it was crazy. It'll never work," Verdine told Business Insider. "It's the combination of a target that's never been drugged before, and drugging it in a way that's never been done before. That sounds like compounding risks."

It turns out, Verdine is a pretty persuasive guy. He flew to France, where investors at Sanofi, a large French pharmaceutical company, were intrigued by his bullishness and agreed to pay 50% of his Series A funding round for his startup Warp Drive Bio.

"There was no IP. There was nothing. It was just an idea that we could drug RAS using molecular glue technology, and I had no idea how you might do it," Verdine said.

In 2018, the technology Verdine pioneered at Warp Drive was acquired by Revolution Medicines, where the chemistry was finessed further. Fourteen years after his initial bet, the FDA approved a drug by Revolution last week that does exactly what Verdine imagined.

Former Sen. Ben Sasse has late-stage, metastatic pancreatic cancer. He's been taking the new daily pill and says it helps.

Nikos Frazier/Omaha World-Herald via Getty Images

Former Nebraska Republican Sen. Ben Sasse, who has stage 4 pancreatic cancer, calls Revolution's pill, which he's been taking in a clinical trial, a "miracle" worker for reducing both his pain and dramatically shrinking tumor volume.

"I have much, much less pain than I had four months ago, when I was diagnosed," Sasse told "60 Minutes" in April. "And I have a massive 76% reduction in tumor volume."

For now, the drug, called Rasonque, is chiefly recommended for patients with advanced cancer and is meant to be used after chemotherapy. It costs about $40,000 a month, before insurance, and side effects include rashes, mouth sores, and some diarrhea.

Taking a $450 million bet based on a beliefZaks was confident a cancer vaccine could work. It was just a matter of timing it right for the immune system.

Tal Zaks

For cancer doctor Tal Zaks, former chief medical officer at Moderna, the ambition was similar.

He knew a cancer vaccine could work. It just required the right architecture, asking the right questions, and conducting the right trial at the right time.

Oh, yes, and also lots of cash, including a $450 million deal with Keytruda-maker Merck to co-develop the technology.

"Where the naysayers are right in this regard is that for cancer vaccines, neither mice data nor phase 1 data even are indicative of whether it's going to work, so you're really taking a very large financial bet just based on first principle beliefs," Zaks said.

"The truth is that from a business perspective, this one was tough — it was a high risk, high reward type bet — it required a significant investment of capital."

He knew lots of cancer vaccines had failed before. He was confident there was a way to win, though, if the immune system was called up in the right way and at the right time.

"From a business perspective, this one was tough — it was a high risk, high reward type bet"- Tal Zaks

Moderna's melanoma vaccine harnesses the genetic makeup of each patient's tumor — teaching the body to attack its own unique cancer mutations. It's administered after a patient's initial treatment and is designed to reduce the risk of cancer recurrence.

"That's really the success of Moderna. I was very adamant when we started this at Moderna that we either funded to the end of a randomized phase 2 or it's not worth doing," he said, referring to the mid-stage clinical trial where researchers tested their vaccine against standard methods for preventing relapse.

The results were a "wow," Zaks said, with Moderna's vaccine almost cutting in half the risk of skin cancer recurring. "This is not about curing mice or showing cool data for a scientific publication. This is about getting conclusive proof."

Moderna's new vaccine for melanoma patients is not FDA-approved, but could be on shelves as soon as 2027, pending a positive review. Common side effects include things you'd expect for a vaccine: some fatigue, chills, and mild pain at the injection site.

But there are caveats to this medication, too. It has to be taken in concert with Keytruda, a $12,000 to $25,000 IV immunotherapy. It also has to be used after a person's tumor has already been surgically removed.

40 years of discovery science also helpedA personalized cancer vaccine takes only a few weeks to produce, thanks to advances in genetic sequencing, and mRNA vaccine technology.

Bloomberg/Getty Images

Of course, there were other discoveries along the way that helped shepherd these breakthroughs, including a far better understanding of cancer genetics, a few key technical solutions, and additional cancer drugs that work in concert with the new technologies. In short, decades of plodding, hard work by scientists across the country and around the world.

"It's taken at least 40 years," mRNA vaccine researcher Phil Felgner, a University of California, Irvine professor who helped develop early versions of the lipid nanoparticle technology that powers the new vaccines, said. "It's taken this much time for it to mature."

And the work isn't over. Revolution is testing a pill for lung cancer, and seeing how its drugs might compete head-to-head against chemotherapy. Moderna is testing vaccines for lung, bladder, and kidney cancers.

These are "approaches that, hopefully, over time will have less toxic side effects to patients, and more targeted effects on the cancer," Dr. Christopher Flowers, division head of cancer medicine at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, said.

All accomplished with some new glue and a shot.

"Ideas sound simple once you get it out, and then there's elegance in that," Coveler, the pancreatic cancer doctor, said. "But I think the design and the specificity of these things was in no way easy to figure out."

items.title: CI/CD for AI Agents: Test Decisions, Not Just Code
items.summary: A practical pipeline for testing agent behavior, releasing it safely, and learning from production failures. Your pull request changes three lines in a prompt. The application builds. Unit tests pass. Integration tests pass. The container reaches production without an error. Then the support agent starts refunding orders that should have been escalated. Nothing in the normal pipeline caught it because the code still worked. The request reached the model, the model called a valid tool, and the API returned 200 OK. The failure was in the agent's behavior: it chose the wrong action. This is the main difference between CI/CD for an API and CI/CD for an AI agent. An API pipeline proves that software behaves according to a defined contract. An agent pipeline must also measure decisions that can vary from one run to the next. That does not mean replacing normal software tests. It means adding another layer around them. What normal CI/CD already does well Consider a backend endpoint: POST /refund input:  order ID + reason output: refund record or a defined error We know how to test this. A useful pipeline might: Run unit tests for refund rules. Run integration tests against a database and payment sandbox. Check the API schema. Scan dependencies and the container image. Build one immutable artifact. Deploy it gradually and watch errors and latency. Given the same database state and input, we expect the same status code and response shape. Keep all of this for an agent. Its API, storage, authentication, tool adapters, and deployment still need ordinary tests. But those checks cannot answer the new question: did the agent make a good decision? Here is the difference at a glance: The release unit is bigger than the code An agent’s behavior usually depends on several parts: Treat these parts as one behavior bundle . Version them together for every candidate release. A release record does not need to be complicated. It can start as JSON: { "release": "support-agent-2026-09-04.2", "code_commit": "8c3f1e2", "prompt_version": "refund-policy-v7", "model": "provider/model-version", "temperature": 0.1, "tool_schema_version": "support-tools-v4", "knowledge_snapshot": "policies-2026-09-04", "max_steps": 8, "timeout_seconds": 30 } Now a bad production run can be tied to the exact prompt, model, tools, data, and limits that produced it. Without this record, “roll back the agent” is an unclear instruction. You may roll back the code while leaving the changed prompt or model in place. CI needs recorded scenarios Live systems are poor test fixtures. Customer state changes, documents are updated, and external APIs return different data. If the world changes between runs, you cannot tell whether a score moved because the agent changed or because its inputs did. The fix is to build a small scenario bank. Each scenario contains: the task given to the agent; recorded responses for every tool it may call; the expected outcome; evidence the agent should use; unsafe or irrelevant actions it should avoid; a step, latency, or cost budget. For the refund agent, one scenario could look like this: name: damaged_item_above_auto_refund_limit task: customer_message: "The monitor arrived with a cracked screen." order_id: "order-1042" recorded_tools: get_order: total_usd: 899 delivered_days_ago: 2 get_refund_policy: automatic_refund_limit_usd: 200 damaged_item_action: escalate expected: outcome: escalate_to_human required_evidence: - order total is above automatic refund limit - policy requires escalation forbidden_actions: - issue_refund max_tool_calls: 4 During CI, replace the live tools with replay tools that return this recorded data. The agent should not know it is in a test. It receives the same tool names and response shapes it would see in production. One detail matters: keep expected away from the agent. Only the grader should see it. If the answer key enters the prompt or retrieval context, a high score only proves the agent can repeat the answer it was shown. Grade the result and the path An agent can reach the right answer for the wrong reason. Imagine that the refund agent escalates every order above $500 without reading the policy. It passes the scenario above, but it has not learned the real rule. A later policy change will expose the shortcut. That is why agent CI should grade two things: Outcome: Did the agent choose the correct answer or action? Trajectory: Did it use the right evidence and stay within its limits? Start with deterministic checks whenever possible: PASS  outcome is escalate_to_human PASS  get_refund_policy was called PASS  issue_refund was not called PASS  tool calls <= 4 PASS  estimated cost <= $0.03 These checks are cheap, repeatable, and easy to explain when they fail. items.summary_html:
A practical pipeline for testing agent behavior, releasing it safely, and learning from production failures.

Your pull request changes three lines in a prompt. The application builds. Unit tests pass. Integration tests pass. The container reaches production without an error.

Then the support agent starts refunding orders that should have been escalated.

Nothing in the normal pipeline caught it because the code still worked. The request reached the model, the model called a valid tool, and the API returned 200 OK. The failure was in the agent's behavior: it chose the wrong action.

This is the main difference between CI/CD for an API and CI/CD for an AI agent. An API pipeline proves that software behaves according to a defined contract. An agent pipeline must also measure decisions that can vary from one run to the next.

That does not mean replacing normal software tests. It means adding another layer around them.

What normal CI/CD already does well

Consider a backend endpoint:

POST /refund
input:  order ID + reason
output: refund record or a defined error

We know how to test this. A useful pipeline might:

  1. Run unit tests for refund rules.
  2. Run integration tests against a database and payment sandbox.
  3. Check the API schema.
  4. Scan dependencies and the container image.
  5. Build one immutable artifact.
  6. Deploy it gradually and watch errors and latency.

Given the same database state and input, we expect the same status code and response shape.

Keep all of this for an agent. Its API, storage, authentication, tool adapters, and deployment still need ordinary tests. But those checks cannot answer the new question: did the agent make a good decision?

Here is the difference at a glance:

The release unit is bigger than the code

An agent’s behavior usually depends on several parts:

Treat these parts as one behavior bundle. Version them together for every candidate release.

A release record does not need to be complicated. It can start as JSON:

{
  "release": "support-agent-2026-09-04.2",
  "code_commit": "8c3f1e2",
  "prompt_version": "refund-policy-v7",
  "model": "provider/model-version",
  "temperature": 0.1,
  "tool_schema_version": "support-tools-v4",
  "knowledge_snapshot": "policies-2026-09-04",
  "max_steps": 8,
  "timeout_seconds": 30
}

Now a bad production run can be tied to the exact prompt, model, tools, data, and limits that produced it. Without this record, “roll back the agent” is an unclear instruction. You may roll back the code while leaving the changed prompt or model in place.

CI needs recorded scenarios

Live systems are poor test fixtures. Customer state changes, documents are updated, and external APIs return different data. If the world changes between runs, you cannot tell whether a score moved because the agent changed or because its inputs did.

The fix is to build a small scenario bank. Each scenario contains:

  • the task given to the agent;
  • recorded responses for every tool it may call;
  • the expected outcome;
  • evidence the agent should use;
  • unsafe or irrelevant actions it should avoid;
  • a step, latency, or cost budget.

For the refund agent, one scenario could look like this:

name: damaged_item_above_auto_refund_limit

task:
  customer_message: "The monitor arrived with a cracked screen."
  order_id: "order-1042"

recorded_tools:
  get_order:
    total_usd: 899
    delivered_days_ago: 2
  get_refund_policy:
    automatic_refund_limit_usd: 200
    damaged_item_action: escalate

expected:
  outcome: escalate_to_human
  required_evidence:
    - order total is above automatic refund limit
    - policy requires escalation
  forbidden_actions:
    - issue_refund
  max_tool_calls: 4

During CI, replace the live tools with replay tools that return this recorded data. The agent should not know it is in a test. It receives the same tool names and response shapes it would see in production.

One detail matters: keep expected away from the agent. Only the grader should see it. If the answer key enters the prompt or retrieval context, a high score only proves the agent can repeat the answer it was shown.

Grade the result and the path

An agent can reach the right answer for the wrong reason. Imagine that the refund agent escalates every order above $500 without reading the policy. It passes the scenario above, but it has not learned the real rule. A later policy change will expose the shortcut.

That is why agent CI should grade two things:

  1. Outcome: Did the agent choose the correct answer or action?
  2. Trajectory: Did it use the right evidence and stay within its limits?

Start with deterministic checks whenever possible:

PASS  outcome is escalate_to_human
PASS  get_refund_policy was called
PASS  issue_refund was not called
PASS  tool calls <= 4
PASS  estimated cost <= $0.03

These checks are cheap, repeatable, and easy to explain when they fail.

Use an LLM judge only for properties that need judgment, such as whether an explanation is clear or whether a response addresses the customer’s concern. Give the judge a narrow rubric and store its comments, but do not let one judge score decide the release by itself. Judge models can vary too.

Do not hide everything behind one score

Suppose version A passes 92% of scenarios and version B passes 94%. Version B looks better until you notice that it doubled cost and occasionally attempts a write action outside policy.

Track separate release dimensions:

Some gates should be absolute. A forbidden payment or deletion action should block the release even when the average quality score improves.

Also run variable scenarios more than once. A single pass tells you what happened once. It does not tell you how often the agent succeeds.

A practical pull-request pipeline

You do not need hundreds of cases on day one. Start with ten to twenty cases that cover the important paths and the failures you fear most.

A useful CI pipeline runs in this order:

1. Lint and type-check

2. Unit-test deterministic code

3. Test tool adapters and schemas

4. Replay the fast scenario suite

5. Compare candidate metrics with the current baseline

6. Run slower or model-based evaluation for risky changes

7. Save the behavior bundle and evaluation report

Run the fast, deterministic suite on every pull request. You can reserve larger or more expensive evaluations for changes to prompts, models, tools, retrieval, or safety policy.

The report should make regressions easy to inspect. Show which scenarios changed, which gate failed, the tool trajectory, token and cost totals, and the candidate’s bundle versions. A single red score with no evidence sends the team back to manual guesswork.

Passing CI should not mean full deployment

A scenario bank only covers cases you already know. Production will find the missing ones.

Release the candidate to a constrained canary first: a small, controlled share of real traffic that limits damage if the new version is wrong. Depending on the agent, that might mean:

  • internal users only;
  • 1% of eligible conversations;
  • read-only tools;
  • a small set of low-risk actions;
  • human approval before any write;
  • tighter step and spending limits.

Compare the canary with the current version. Watch task success, escalation rate, forbidden actions, tool errors, latency, cost, and user corrections. Keep the previous behavior bundle ready for rollback.

The blast radius should match your confidence. A summarization agent can usually take a larger canary than an agent that changes account permissions.

Store traces you can actually investigate

HTTP metrics are still useful, but 200 OK does not mean the agent did the right thing. For each run, record enough information to reconstruct the decision:

  • behavior bundle version;
  • scenario, request, or session ID;
  • model and prompt version;
  • tools called, arguments, and results;
  • outcome;
  • policy decisions and human approvals;
  • tokens, latency, and estimated cost;
  • user correction, escalation, or rollback signal.

Apply access controls and retention limits. Redact secrets and personal data before storing traces or turning them into test scenarios. Evaluation data can become a second copy of production data if you treat it carelessly.

Turn production misses into regression tests

The scenario bank should grow from real failures, not only imagined edge cases.

When the agent makes a meaningful mistake:

  1. Save the trace and confirm what should have happened.
  2. Remove secrets and unnecessary customer data.
  3. Replace live tool calls with recorded responses.
  4. Write an answer key and safety limits.
  5. Reproduce the failure against the released bundle.
  6. Fix the agent and keep the scenario in CI permanently.

This is the same habit that makes an ordinary test suite valuable: a bug should be paid for once. After the fix, the pipeline remembers it.

The minimum useful version

If all of this feels like too much, build the first version in this order:

  1. Version the prompt, model, tools, and budgets with the code.
  2. Record five real tasks whose correct outcomes you know.
  3. Replay tool responses instead of calling live systems.
  4. Check outcome, required evidence, forbidden actions, and step count.
  5. Compare every candidate with the released baseline.
  6. Deploy to a read-only or human-approved canary.
  7. Turn the next production miss into scenario number six.

That is enough to stop deciding whether a prompt change “feels better.”

The complete delivery loop is:

Change → replay → evaluate → compare → canary → observe → record → repeat

Normal CI/CD still ships the application. The added agent pipeline gives you evidence that the behavior inside it is ready to ship too.

items.title: I told the model to separate fields with <TAB>. It did exactly that, and I lost 79 percent of my data.
items.summary:
My extraction prompt said: Output lines of the form The model output: Elizabeth I have not the pleasure of understanding you Those are five literal characters — angle bracket, T, A, B, angle bracket — not a tab. My parser looked for \t , found none, and dropped the line. Across one document, 246 of 310 records were discarded . Only 5 were dropped for the reason the mechanism actually existed to catch. The model did what I asked. I asked for the wrong thing. Why I did not notice for a whole benchmark run This is the part worth stealing, because the bug is trivial and the reason it survived is not. My harness counted discarded records in a single field called rejected . That field had one documented meaning: a record whose evidence could not be verified against the source text . In other words, it was the hallucination-catching counter. So the run printed rejected=246 and I read it as the verifier working hard . A parser failure was wearing the costume of a successful integrity check. The number went up, and up was the direction I wanted. The fix is not a better parser. It is that these two things must never share a counter: unparseable — our format failed, the model is not at fault ungrounded — the model asserted something that is not in the text One of those is my bug. The other is the model's. Summing them produces a number that cannot be acted on, and which flatters whichever explanation you already believe. After splitting them, the same run reads: records: lines=310 kept=64 | unparseable=246 ungrounded=5
separator: canonical=0 tab=64 literal_TAB=246 There is no way to misread that. Fix one: show the delimiter, never name it A model can reproduce a character it can see. It cannot reliably reproduce a character you have described in prose, because your description is text and copying text is what it does. So instead of naming the separator, I showed a worked example using a pipe. I picked | after checking the corpus contained zero of them in 7,987,517 characters. Result: canonical separator compliance went from 0 to 9 out of 9 on the first fragment, and unparseable loss went from 79 percent to zero. Fix two: your example must be obviously not data The first version of that fix failed differently, and worse. I used a real line from the source novel as the worked example: Elizabeth | I have not the pleasure of understanding you The model copied the example verbatim and extracted nothing else. One line of output for a 60,000-character fragment. It looked plausible. The name was a real character, the quote was real dialogue. The only reason I caught it was that the evidence verifier rejected it — that sentence is not in the fragment I sent, it is from a later chapter. The working version uses a name that cannot appear in any novel and says so: Zolvane | we must leave before the tide turns

That line is ONLY a format example. Zolvane is not in this text; never copy
the example into your answer. A worked example is an instruction to imitate. If your example is indistinguishable from valid output, some fraction of the time it will be returned as output. Fix three: make the failure loud, at the right granularity I added a check that aborts when more than 20 percent of output lines have no recognised separator, printing a sample of the offending line. My first version aborted the whole document. That was worse than the bug: the model follows the format on most fragments and abandons it on a few, so discarding the document threw away every good fragment along with the bad one. Four documents produced zero records. Now a violation fails one fragment . Good fragments survive, the failure is still visible and still blocks a headline answer, and one document went from zero records to 148 of 169 kept. The forty-second diagnostic The single highest-value thing I added was a --probe flag: run one fragment, print the raw model reply verbatim, print the loss breakdown, exit. It takes about seven seconds. It caught both the literal- bug and the example-copying bug immediately. Before that, my shortest path to noticing a contract problem was a full benchmark run — about forty minutes — and even then only if I read the right counter and interpreted it correctly, which the first time around I did not. If your pipeline sends prompts to a model in a loop, you want a way to see exactly one of them, unedited, in under a minute. I wrote three throwaway scripts to do that by hand before admitting it should be a flag.

items.title: GPA Scales Do Not Convert. Building a Calculator That Admits It.
items.summary:
GPA Scales Do Not Convert. Building a Calculator That Admits It. Every GPA calculator eventually gets the same feature request: "can you convert my 8.6/10 to a 4.0 GPA?" The obvious implementation is one line: const converted = ( gpa / fromMax ) * toMax ; // wrong, and confidently so This is linear rescaling, and it is wrong for a reason that has nothing to do with arithmetic: the scales are not measuring the same thing at the same resolution. What the scales actually are A grading scale is a mapping from letter or percentage bands to numbers. The bands are not evenly spaced, and they are not the same across systems: US 4.0        A = 4.0    B = 3.0    C = 2.0    D = 1.0    F = 0
              (a letter covers ~10 percentage points, roughly linear)

India 10.0    often  CGPA ≈ percentage / 9.5,  but institution-specific
              (the divisor is a convention, not a conversion)

France 20.0   14/20 is a strong result; 18/20 is exceptional and rare
              (the top of the scale is deliberately almost unreachable) Rescaling a French 14/20 linearly gives 2.8 on a 4.0 scale — a US "B−". Anyone familiar with both systems will tell you a 14/20 is a considerably better result than that. The error is not in the multiplication; it is in assuming both scales use their full range the same way. French grading compresses the top deliberately. US 4.0 grading does not. The same applies going the other way. A 10.0-scale CGPA of 8.6 mapped linearly is 3.44, but many Indian institutions publish a conversion of CGPA × 9.5 = percentage , which gives 81.7% — and 81.7% is not a 3.44 in most US conversion tables either. So what should a calculator do? The honest answer is: compute within a scale, and be loud about conversion between them. Within a scale , GPA is well-defined and worth computing precisely: it is Σ(grade_points × credits) / Σ(credits) , and the only real complexity is credit
weighting and how the institution rounds. Between scales , there is no universally correct function. There are institutional
conversion tables, and they disagree with each other. A calculator that silently applies linear rescaling is producing a number that looks authoritative and is not. One that supports multiple scales natively — 4.0, 4.3, 4.5, 5.0, 7.0, 10.0, 20-point, percentage — lets a student compute in the system they are actually graded in, which is the number they actually need. The weighting bug that is much more common Conversion is the flashy problem. The bug that bites more people is credit weighting. // wrong: unweighted mean, ignores credit hours const gpa = grades . reduce (( a , g ) => a + g , 0 ) / grades . length ; // right: credit-weighted mean const gpa = courses . reduce (( a , c ) => a + c . points * c . credits , 0 ) / courses . reduce (( a , c ) => a + c . credits , 0 ); The two agree only when every course carries identical credits — which is true in some high school systems and false in essentially every university. A student taking a 1-credit seminar and a 4-credit core course does not have those two grades count equally, and a calculator that says otherwise gives a number the registrar will never produce. Then there is weighted vs unweighted in the US high school sense, which is a completely different meaning of "weighted": AP/honours courses map an A to 5.0 instead of 4.0. Both concepts are real, both are called weighting, and conflating them in the UI produces support emails forever. They need different words in the interface. Rounding is a policy, not a detail 3.4950 displayed as 3.50 versus 3.49 decides scholarship eligibility at some institutions. There is no neutral choice here: Round half up, round half even, or truncate — all three are in real use Round once at the end, or round each semester and then average the rounded values —
these give different answers Some institutions cap the displayed GPA at the scale maximum, some let weighted values
exceed it A calculator cannot know which policy applies. What it can do is not hide the choice: show enough decimal places that the user can see they are near a boundary, rather than silently rounding them across it. What I would tell someone building one Compute the credit-weighted mean. Always. The unweighted version is a different
statistic and almost never the one asked for. Support scales natively instead of converting into one canonical scale internally.
Round-tripping through a canonical scale loses information at every hop. If you offer conversion at all, label it as an estimate and say which table you used. Use different words for "credit-weighted" and "AP/honours weighted" in the UI. They are
unrelated concepts that share a name. Show one more decimal place than you think you need. Boundary cases matter more than
precision looks like it should. None of this is difficult code. It is mostly the discipline of not producing a number that is more confident than the underlying data supports — which, for a tool students use to make decisions about their applications, seems like the minimum bar. If you want the credit-weighted version without writing it yourself, the calculator is here — it computes on the scale you are actually graded on rather than converting you into one.

Rounding is a policy, not a detail

3.4950 displayed as 3.50 versus 3.49 decides scholarship eligibility at some
institutions. There is no neutral choice here:

  • Round half up, round half even, or truncate — all three are in real use
  • Round once at the end, or round each semester and then average the rounded values — these give different answers
  • Some institutions cap the displayed GPA at the scale maximum, some let weighted values exceed it

A calculator cannot know which policy applies. What it can do is not hide the choice: show
enough decimal places that the user can see they are near a boundary, rather than
silently rounding them across it.

What I would tell someone building one
  • Compute the credit-weighted mean. Always. The unweighted version is a different statistic and almost never the one asked for.
  • Support scales natively instead of converting into one canonical scale internally. Round-tripping through a canonical scale loses information at every hop.
  • If you offer conversion at all, label it as an estimate and say which table you used.
  • Use different words for "credit-weighted" and "AP/honours weighted" in the UI. They are unrelated concepts that share a name.
  • Show one more decimal place than you think you need. Boundary cases matter more than precision looks like it should.

None of this is difficult code. It is mostly the discipline of not producing a number
that is more confident than the underlying data supports — which, for a tool students use
to make decisions about their applications, seems like the minimum bar.

If you want the credit-weighted version without writing it yourself,
the calculator is here — it computes on the scale you are
actually graded on rather than converting you into one.

They give us a clearer way to understand the impact of a particular change. Do not recommend a more expensive flight when a cheaper eligible flight exists."} {"id": "find_cheapest_flight", "query": "What is the cheapest flight from Bangalore to Tokyo tomorrow?", "expected_behavior": "Recommend the lowest-priced retrieved flight for the requested route and date."} The first case asks: Did we improve the behavior we were trying to change? Running the Experiment Locally If you’ve been following the series and already have Wayfinder set up locally, you can skip the installation and environment setup below. Just make sure you’re on the version used for this experiment. The complete implementation used throughout this article is available in the companion GitHub repository . To follow along with exactly the same code shown in this article, check out the v0.6.0 release. This ensures the code, commands and screenshots remain consistent over time. To follow along locally, clone the repository and check out the release containing the online evaluation implementation: git clone https://github.com/DivakarUngatla/wayfinder.git cd wayfinder git checkout v0.6.0 Install the project dependencies: uv sync Before running the evaluation, configure the required environment variables. Create a .env file: cp .env.example .env Configure the required environment variables: OPENAI_API_KEY= LANGSMITH_API_KEY= LANGSMITH_TRACING=true Running Evaluations as Experiments We now have a fixed set of examples. An experiment is a recorded evaluation run of a particular version of our application against a fixed dataset. For each example, the experiment: runs the application captures its response and the context it used evaluates that response records the results Later, after we change the application, we’ll repeat the same experiment with the same evaluation setup and compare the results.
