LangSmith gives it an example from our dataset, and Wayfinder returns both the generated response and the flights it retrieved. The evaluator then takes that output and scores it against the expected behavior. We’re reusing the same LLM-as-a-Judge evaluator we built earlier in the series, so we’re not introducing a new evaluation technique here. We’re changing how we use the evaluation results: instead of looking at one run in isolation, we’re going to compare runs from different versions of the application. The target runs Wayfinder. The evaluator scores its behavior. And LangSmith records the results as an experiment that we can inspect and compare later. There is one parameter here that deserves some attention: num_repetitions=args.repetitions Why would we run the same evaluation example more than once? Because with an AI application, one successful run doesn’t necessarily mean the behavior is consistently correct. And that’s something our baseline experiment is about to show us. Establishing Our Baseline Before making any changes to the application, we need to understand how the current version behaves. This gives us our baseline — the reference point we’ll compare our change against later. We’ll run the two examples in our dataset five times each: python examples/experiment_comparison/compare_experiments.py \ --dataset-name wayfinder_experiment_comparison \ --prefix wayfinder-baseline \ --repetitions 5 The first time we run this command, the experiment runner creates the dataset in LangSmith from our local JSONL file. From then on, we’ll reuse this same dataset for every experiment in this article. With two examples and five repetitions, our baseline contains 10 evaluation runs . Why repeat each example five times instead of evaluating it once? Because a single successful response can give us a false sense of confidence. AI applications can produce different responses for the same input, and our LLM-based evaluator can vary as well. If a behavior works once, we know it can work. If it works repeatedly, we start learning something about how consistently it works. When the evaluation completes, the runner prints a link to the experiment in LangSmith. Let’s open it and look at what happened across the five repetitions. The simple cheapest-flight request works correctly in all five runs. The multi-constraint request is different: four repetitions score perfectly, but one fails. In repetition 3, Wayfinder recommends Japan Airlines JL703 at ₹48,550 with 12 available seats . But the retrieved flights also contain Air India AI302 at ₹41,000 with 6 available seats . Air India satisfies the same minimum-seat requirement and is cheaper. Wayfinder had the information it needed, but still selected the wrong flight. Your exact results may differ. Both the application and the LLM-based evaluator are non-deterministic, so you may see the incorrect recommendation in a different repetition — or all five runs may succeed. What matters is that we use the same evaluation setup when comparing the baseline with the version we change next. The interesting part isn’t that Wayfinder cannot handle the request — it gets it right in four of the five runs. The problem is that the same request doesn’t produce consistently correct behavior . Now we have something concrete to improve — and something concrete to compare our next experiment against. Finding the Right Thing to Change Our baseline showed us where the application sometimes fails. But before changing anything, we need to understand why . In the failed run, Wayfinder had already retrieved the cheaper Air India flight. So retrieval wasn’t the problem. The problem happens after retrieval. In the current implementation, the retrieved flights are passed to the response-generation LLM. The LLM has to apply the user’s constraints, compare the eligible flights, select the cheapest one and generate the final response. Conceptually, the flow looks like this: Retrieved Flights ↓ LLM ↓ Apply constraints Compare prices Generate response But filtering by available seats and comparing prices are deterministic operations. We don’t need an LLM to make those decisions. That gives us a simple engineering hypothesis: Move deterministic filtering and ranking into application code, and let the LLM focus on generating the response. The application would then look more like: Retrieved Flights ↓ Filter + Rank ↓ LLM ↓ Generate response We don’t know yet whether this change will actually improve the application. That’s exactly what our next experiment will measure. Moving Deterministic Decisions into Application Code Now we can implement our hypothesis. Wayfinder already uses an LLM to convert the user’s request into a structured FlightSearchRequest. We can extend that structure so the application also knows how the results should be ranked: passengers: int = Field(default=1) sort_by: Literal["price", "duration"] | None = None arrival_before: time | None = None For our target request: Find the cheapest flight from Bangalore to Tokyo tomorrow with at least 2 available seats. the extraction step now produces: { "source": "Bangalore", "destination": "Tokyo", "passengers": 2, "sort_by": "price", "arrival_before": null } The LLM is still doing something it’s good at: turning natural language into structured intent . But once we have that structure, the application can handle the deterministic decisions itself: flights = [ flight for flight in flights if flight.available_seats >= request.passengers ] if request.sort_by == "price": flights.sort(key=lambda flight: flight.price) elif request.sort_by == "duration": flights.sort(key=lambda flight: flight.duration) For our target request, this means Wayfinder first removes flights with fewer than two available seats and then sorts the remaining flights by price. The response-generation LLM no longer needs to perform that filtering or ranking itself. It receives flights that have already been processed according to the structured request and focuses on generating the response. So our architecture has shifted from: LLM → interpret constraints + make deterministic decisions + respond to: LLM → structured intent → deterministic application logic → LLM response The change looks promising, but we haven’t established that it actually improves the application’s behavior. To find out, we’ll run the same evaluation again and compare the two experiments We’ve only looked at the key parts of the change here. The complete implementation also handles additional filtering and ranking behavior and updates the response-generation flow accordingly. If you’re following along with the repository, switch back to the main branch to get the completed candidate implementation: git checkout main git pull This gives us the candidate version we’ll evaluate next. Our v0.6.0 checkout remains the reproducible baseline we started with. Running the Candidate Experiment Now we evaluate the changed application using exactly the same setup as our baseline . Same dataset. Same two examples. Same evaluator. Same five repetitions. The only thing we’ve changed is the application itself. Run: uv run python examples/experiment_comparison/compare_experiments.py \ --dataset-name wayfinder_experiment_comparison \ --prefix wayfinder-deterministic-filtering \ --repetitions 5 The runner creates a second experiment in LangSmith, this time using our candidate implementation. Now let’s look at the same multi-constraint request that failed once in our baseline: Find the cheapest flight from Bangalore to Tokyo tomorrow with at least 2 available seats. This time, all five repetitions receive a score of 5 across every evaluation criterion . In our baseline, the same request succeeded in four repetitions but selected the wrong flight in one. After moving filtering and ranking into deterministic application logic, we don’t see that failure in any of the five candidate repetitions. That’s encouraging — but looking at the candidate experiment by itself still doesn’t answer the question we started this article with. Did our change actually make the application better overall? For that, we need to compare the baseline and candidate experiments directly. Comparing the Experiments Now we can finally put the two experiments side by side. Both experiments used the same dataset, evaluator, and five repetitions per example . The only thing we intentionally changed was the application. LangSmith lets us compare the results directly: For our multi-constraint request, the difference is immediately visible. The baseline’s failed repetition pulled several evaluation scores down. In the candidate experiment, every criterion scores 5.00 across all five repetitions . More importantly, the behavior changed: we no longer observed the incorrect flight selection, while our simpler cheapest-flight regression guard continued to work correctly. The behavior we targeted improved, while the behavior we wanted to protect did not regress. This doesn’t prove the application will behave correctly for every request. But with the same dataset, evaluator, and repetitions on both sides, we now have evidence that our change improved the behavior we set out to fix. That’s what experiment comparison gives us: evidence for an engineering decision. Conclusion In this article, we explored how evaluation experiments can help us answer a question that comes up constantly when building AI applications: Did my change actually make the application better? We built a focused evaluation dataset, established a baseline across repeated runs, made a targeted application change, and evaluated the candidate using the same setup. By comparing the two experiments, we could see whether the behavior we wanted to improve actually got better while also checking that existing behavior didn’t regress. This gives us a repeatable engineering loop for changing AI applications: Baseline → Change → Evaluate → Compare → Decide Whether we’re changing prompts, models, retrieval, tools, or application logic, experiment comparison gives us evidence to understand the impact of those changes instead of relying on intuition or a few successful examplesison gives us a way to answer that question with evidence. What’s Next? With experiment comparison, we’ve completed the AI Evaluation track of AI Engineering Fundamentals . Across this series, we’ve moved from understanding why traditional software tests aren’t enough for AI applications to building rule-based, human, LLM-based, and online evaluation workflows — and finally to using those evaluations to measure the impact of application changes. Next, we’ll move on to the next area of AI engineering. AI Evaluation Series This article completes our AI Evaluation series, covering the journey from evaluation fundamentals to measuring and improving real-world AI applications. ✅ Part 1: Software Tests vs AI Evals ✅ Part 2: Understanding AI Evaluation ✅ Part 3: Rule-Based Evaluation ✅ Part 4: Human Evaluation ✅ Part 5: LLM-as-a-Judge ✅ Part 6: Online Evaluation ✅ Part 7: Comparing Evaluation Experiments Comparing AI Evaluation Experiments: Measuring the Impact of Changes to AI Applications was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

This time, all five repetitions receive a score of 5 across every evaluation criterion.

In our baseline, the same request succeeded in four repetitions but selected the wrong flight in one. After moving filtering and ranking into deterministic application logic, we don’t see that failure in any of the five candidate repetitions.

That’s encouraging — but looking at the candidate experiment by itself still doesn’t answer the question we started this article with.

Did our change actually make the application better overall?

For that, we need to compare the baseline and candidate experiments directly.

Comparing the Experiments

Now we can finally put the two experiments side by side.

Both experiments used the same dataset, evaluator, and five repetitions per example. The only thing we intentionally changed was the application.

LangSmith lets us compare the results directly:

For our multi-constraint request, the difference is immediately visible.

The baseline’s failed repetition pulled several evaluation scores down. In the candidate experiment, every criterion scores 5.00 across all five repetitions.

More importantly, the behavior changed: we no longer observed the incorrect flight selection, while our simpler cheapest-flight regression guard continued to work correctly.

The behavior we targeted improved, while the behavior we wanted to protect did not regress.

This doesn’t prove the application will behave correctly for every request. But with the same dataset, evaluator, and repetitions on both sides, we now have evidence that our change improved the behavior we set out to fix.

That’s what experiment comparison gives us: evidence for an engineering decision.

Conclusion

In this article, we explored how evaluation experiments can help us answer a question that comes up constantly when building AI applications:

Did my change actually make the application better?

We built a focused evaluation dataset, established a baseline across repeated runs, made a targeted application change, and evaluated the candidate using the same setup.

By comparing the two experiments, we could see whether the behavior we wanted to improve actually got better while also checking that existing behavior didn’t regress.

This gives us a repeatable engineering loop for changing AI applications:

Baseline → Change → Evaluate → Compare → Decide

Whether we’re changing prompts, models, retrieval, tools, or application logic, experiment comparison gives us evidence to understand the impact of those changes instead of relying on intuition or a few successful examplesison gives us a way to answer that question with evidence.

What’s Next?

With experiment comparison, we’ve completed the AI Evaluation track of AI Engineering Fundamentals.

Across this series, we’ve moved from understanding why traditional software tests aren’t enough for AI applications to building rule-based, human, LLM-based, and online evaluation workflows — and finally to using those evaluations to measure the impact of application changes.

Next, we’ll move on to the next area of AI engineering.

AI Evaluation Series

This article completes our AI Evaluation series, covering the journey from evaluation fundamentals to measuring and improving real-world AI applications.

items.summary:
When we examine the modern enterprise AI landscape, we frequently encounter a common paradox: while generative AI promises to revolutionize customer support, internal search, and knowledge management, the underlying infrastructure required to deploy these solutions often grows prohibitively complex. Historically, building a production-grade Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline meant provisioning specialized external vector databases, managing intricate data synchronization pipelines, and risking data sprawl across ungoverned cloud environments. We realized that for many enterprise workloads, this massive infrastructure overhead is entirely unnecessary. By leveraging Microsoft Fabric ’s unified data estate, native Apache Spark engine, and Delta Lake storage format, we can build a fully operational, enterprise-grade RAG solution directly on top of our existing OneLake data. In this detailed operational guide, we share how we designed and deployed an end-to-end vector embedding and retrieval system using fewer than 50 lines of PySpark and Python code, connecting Azure OpenAI directly to our governed customer transcripts without moving a single byte outside our analytical perimeter. Architecture: OneLake → PySpark Vectorization → Azure OpenAI Our primary goal was to design an architecture that maximizes simplicity, security, and query execution performance while operating entirely within our governed workspace. Rather than exporting unstructured transcripts to a third-party vector database, we construct a unified pipeline where storage, compute, and AI inference coexist seamlessly. Our end-to-end RAG workflow follows a structured four-stage continuum: Governed Storage Layer (OneLake & Delta Parquet): Our raw and processed datasets, such as customer support logs, operational records, or internal knowledge bases reside directly within our Lakehouse as open Delta Parquet tables. This guarantees ACID compliance, version history, and zero-copy accessibility across analytical engines. Distributed Vectorization Engine (PySpark & Pandas UDFs): We harness Fabric’s native Apache Spark compute cluster to distribute the task of generating vector embeddings across millions of text records simultaneously. By employing PyArrow-accelerated Pandas UDFs, we batch API requests to Azure OpenAI efficiently. In-Lake Vector Persistence: Vector embeddings are stored natively as array columns inside a dedicated Gold Delta table (Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors). This eliminates external database licensing costs and guarantees that vector updates maintain strict transactional synchronization with our source tables. Distributed Vector Retrieval & Downstream Serving: We query our vectorized Delta tables directly using high-performance Spark mathematical expressions to extract relevant context segments, which are then passed alongside user prompts to Azure OpenAI or surfaced through interactive interfaces. Generating Embeddings: Distributed Processing with Pandas UDFs To transform raw, unstructured text into dense vector representations, we must process large volumes of data efficiently. Calling an external embedding API row-by-row in a traditional loop introduces severe latency bottlenecks and exhausts network bandwidth. To resolve this, we leverage PySpark’s vectorized Pandas User Defined Functions (@pandas_udf). Pandas UDFs utilize Apache Arrow to transfer data seamlessly between Spark JVM memory and Python worker processes without the performance penalty of standard Python serialization. This allows us to process incoming text series in batched chunks, optimizing worker throughput and stabilizing API call patterns. Below is the exact implementation we designed to read customer support transcripts from OneLake, generate 1536-dimensional vector embeddings using Azure OpenAI, and persist the results back into our Gold Lakehouse layer: # PySpark Notebook in Fabric: Creating Vector Embeddings for OneLake Text Data import openai from pyspark.sql.functions import pandas_udf, col import pandas as pd # Set Azure OpenAI Config openai.api_type = "azure" openai.api_base = "https://your-resource.openai.azure.com/" openai.api_key = "YOUR_KEY" # Define a Pandas UDF for batch embedding generation @pandas_udf("array ") def generate_embeddings(text_series: pd.Series) -> pd.Series: def get_embedding(text): response = openai.Embedding.create( input=text, engine="text-embedding-ada-002" ) return response['data'][0]['embedding'] return text_series.apply(get_embedding) ' # Read customer support logs from OneLake df_logs = spark.read.table("Gold_Lakehouse.CustomerSupportTranscripts") # Generate embeddings and save as a new Delta table for vector search df_vectorized = df_logs.withColumn("VectorEmbedding", generate_embeddings(col("TranscriptText"))) df_vectorized.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors") Deconstructing the Vectorization Pipeline Let us examine the mechanical steps executed by this concise script: Environment Configuration: We initialize our Azure OpenAI credentials and endpoint configurations directly within our secure Fabric Notebook execution session. Vectorized UDF Definition: By decorating our function with @pandas_udf("array "), we instruct PySpark that the output column will be structured as an array of floating-point values. The inner function accepts a pandas.Series containing text fragments and dispatches API requests to the text-embedding-ada-002 model. Reading Governed Delta Tables: We invoke spark.read.table("Gold_Lakehouse.CustomerSupportTranscripts") to fetch our curated support transcripts natively from OneLake. Fabric abstracts away underlying ABFSS file paths and partition handling automatically. Distributed Transformation: When we execute withColumn("VectorEmbedding", generate_embeddings(...)), PySpark distributes the workload across the active Spark cluster nodes. Each executor node processes a slice of the dataset in parallel, sending batched requests to Azure OpenAI. Atomic Delta Lake Persistence: Finally, we persist the vectorized DataFrame back into OneLake using .write.format("delta").saveAsTable("Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors"). Because Delta Lake provides strict ACID transaction guarantees, our vectorized dataset remains resilient against partial failures during write operations. Vector Search: Querying Embeddings Using PySpark & Math Functions Once our text embeddings are persisted in OneLake, we require a method to identify the most relevant customer transcripts when an incoming user query arrives. In traditional RAG setups, this step relies on dedicated vector databases using index structures like HNSW or IVF. However, for datasets containing hundreds of thousands to millions of rows, we can compute mathematical similarity directly within PySpark using vector geometry. Cosine similarity is the gold standard metric for measuring semantic closeness between high-dimensional text embeddings. Conceptually, it evaluates the angle between two vectors, such as an incoming user query and a stored document to determine how similar they are in context. Distributed Vector Lookup in PySpark We can implement this similarity lookup natively by taking an incoming user prompt, generating its vector representation, and computing the dot product against our vector column stored in Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors: # PySpark Vector Retrieval Code import numpy as np from pyspark.sql.functions import udf, col from pyspark.sql.types import FloatType # 1. Generate query embedding for user prompt user_prompt = "How do I reset my customer portal password?" prompt_response = openai.Embedding.create(input=user_prompt, engine="text-embedding-ada-002") query_vector = prompt_response['data'][0]['embedding'] # 2. Define a cosine similarity / dot product UDF @udf(returnType=FloatType()) def compute_similarity(doc_vector): if doc_vector is None: return 0.0 return float(np.dot(query_vector, doc_vector)) # 3. Query vectors from OneLake and retrieve top 5 matches df_vectors = spark.read.table("Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors") top_matches = ( df_vectors .withColumn("Similarity", compute_similarity(col("VectorEmbedding"))) .orderBy(col("Similarity").desc()) .limit(5) ) # Collect top context documents retrieved_docs = [row['TranscriptText'] for row in top_matches.collect()] By executing this transformation across our Spark cluster, we perform candidate vector retrieval directly inside our analytical Lakehouse engine. The process retrieves the most contextually relevant transcript segments within milliseconds, perfectly preparing our pipeline for the generative synthesis stage. Serving and Orchestration: Synthesizing Context and Deployment With our vector retrieval engine operational, the final component of our enterprise RAG pipeline is prompt orchestration and response generation. We synthesize the retrieved transcript passages into a grounded context window and submit the instruction to Azure OpenAI Chat Completions. # Construct grounded context prompt context_block = "
---
".join(retrieved_docs) system_instruction = ( "We are an AI assistant designed to answer customer support queries based strictly on historic logs. " "Use only the provided context to answer the prompt accurately." ) # Call Azure OpenAI Chat Completion completion_response = openai.ChatCompletion.create( engine="gpt-4", messages=[ {"role": "system", "content": system_instruction}, {"role": "user", "content": f"Context:
{context_block}

Question: {user_prompt}"} ] ) final_answer = completion_response['choices'][0]['message']['content'] print(final_answer) Deployment Patterns: Gradio and Copilot Studio Integrations To bring this RAG solution into production and surface it to business stakeholders across our organization, we evaluate two highly effective serving patterns: Embedded Interactive Interfaces in Fabric: For internal prototyping, testing, or technical user interfaces, we can wrap our retrieval and synthesis functions into a lightweight Gradio interface running directly within a Fabric Notebook session. This allows analysts to test context retrieval, adjust hyper-parameters, and evaluate model grounding in real time. Copilot Studio & Semantic Link Orchestration: For enterprise-wide deployment, we can expose our PySpark RAG execution logic as an automated backend endpoint or register our Lakehouse tables within Power BI semantic models using Semantic Link (sempy). Copilot Studio can then query these semantic layers and invoke our underlying vectorized tables seamlessly, providing business users with an AI agent that converses with governed enterprise data in real time. Production Considerations: Performance, Cost, and Governance As we transition our concise PySpark RAG pipeline into a continuous production environment, we incorporate several critical engineering practices to maintain operational efficiency and low compute cost: Storage Optimization with V-Order: When saving our vectorized Delta tables in OneLake, we ensure that Microsoft’s proprietary V-Order compression is enabled. V-Order reorganizes Parquet files at write time, dramatically improving memory layout and accelerating downstream read speeds when Spark or SQL engines scan vector arrays. Incremental Embeddings via Change Data Capture (CDC): Rather than re-generating embeddings for our entire dataset during every run, we implement incremental processing using Delta Lake transaction logs. By inspecting modified rows, we only vectorize newly inserted or updated customer transcripts, reducing OpenAI API overhead substantially. Unified Data Governance & Security: Because our embeddings reside within native OneLake Delta tables, they inherit Microsoft Purview governance policies, row-level security, and access controls automatically. Sensitive customer information remains fully safeguarded without requiring complex vector database role-based access configurations. Conclusion By unifying our storage layer, distributed compute, vector geometry, and generative AI orchestration within Microsoft Fabric , we eliminate the friction of managing external infrastructure. In under 50 lines of Python code, we constructed a resilient, enterprise-grade RAG pipeline that operates entirely on top of open Delta Parquet tables in OneLake. This architecture keeps our enterprise data fully governed, minimizes total cost of ownership, and accelerates our time-to-value when deploying generative AI solutions. As we continue to advance our data engineering practices, solutions like this demonstrate that powerful enterprise AI does not require overly complex stacks, only the right unified foundation. When we examine the modern enterprise AI landscape, we frequently encounter a common paradox: while generative AI promises to revolutionize customer support, internal search, and knowledge management, the underlying infrastructure required to deploy these solutions often grows prohibitively complex. Historically, building a production-grade Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline meant provisioning specialized external vector databases, managing intricate data synchronization pipelines, and risking data sprawl across ungoverned cloud environments.

In this detailed operational guide, we share how we designed and deployed an end-to-end vector embedding and retrieval system using fewer than 50 lines of PySpark and Python code, connecting Azure OpenAI directly to our governed customer transcripts without moving a single byte outside our analytical perimeter.

Architecture: OneLake → PySpark Vectorization → Azure OpenAI

Our primary goal was to design an architecture that maximizes simplicity, security, and query execution performance while operating entirely within our governed workspace. Rather than exporting unstructured transcripts to a third-party vector database, we construct a unified pipeline where storage, compute, and AI inference coexist seamlessly.

Our end-to-end RAG workflow follows a structured four-stage continuum:

  • Governed Storage Layer (OneLake & Delta Parquet): Our raw and processed datasets, such as customer support logs, operational records, or internal knowledge bases reside directly within our Lakehouse as open Delta Parquet tables. This guarantees ACID compliance, version history, and zero-copy accessibility across analytical engines.
  • Distributed Vectorization Engine (PySpark & Pandas UDFs): We harness Fabric’s native Apache Spark compute cluster to distribute the task of generating vector embeddings across millions of text records simultaneously. By employing PyArrow-accelerated Pandas UDFs, we batch API requests to Azure OpenAI efficiently.
  • In-Lake Vector Persistence: Vector embeddings are stored natively as array columns inside a dedicated Gold Delta table (Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors). This eliminates external database licensing costs and guarantees that vector updates maintain strict transactional synchronization with our source tables.
  • Distributed Vector Retrieval & Downstream Serving: We query our vectorized Delta tables directly using high-performance Spark mathematical expressions to extract relevant context segments, which are then passed alongside user prompts to Azure OpenAI or surfaced through interactive interfaces.
Generating Embeddings: Distributed Processing with Pandas UDFs

To transform raw, unstructured text into dense vector representations, we must process large volumes of data efficiently. Calling an external embedding API row-by-row in a traditional loop introduces severe latency bottlenecks and exhausts network bandwidth. To resolve this, we leverage PySpark’s vectorized Pandas User Defined Functions (@pandas_udf).

Pandas UDFs utilize Apache Arrow to transfer data seamlessly between Spark JVM memory and Python worker processes without the performance penalty of standard Python serialization. This allows us to process incoming text series in batched chunks, optimizing worker throughput and stabilizing API call patterns.

Below is the exact implementation we designed to read customer support transcripts from OneLake, generate 1536-dimensional vector embeddings using Azure OpenAI, and persist the results back into our Gold Lakehouse layer:

# PySpark Notebook in Fabric: Creating Vector Embeddings for OneLake Text Data
import openai
from pyspark.sql.functions import pandas_udf, col
import pandas as pd

# Set Azure OpenAI Config
openai.api_type = "azure"
openai.api_base = "https://your-resource.openai.azure.com/"
openai.api_key = "YOUR_KEY"

# Define a Pandas UDF for batch embedding generation
@pandas_udf("array")
def generate_embeddings(text_series: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    def get_embedding(text):
        response = openai.Embedding.create(
            input=text, engine="text-embedding-ada-002"
        )
        return response['data'][0]['embedding']
    return text_series.apply(get_embedding)
'
# Read customer support logs from OneLake
df_logs = spark.read.table("Gold_Lakehouse.CustomerSupportTranscripts")

# Generate embeddings and save as a new Delta table for vector search
df_vectorized = df_logs.withColumn("VectorEmbedding", generate_embeddings(col("TranscriptText")))
df_vectorized.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors")
Deconstructing the Vectorization Pipeline

Let us examine the mechanical steps executed by this concise script:

  • Environment Configuration: We initialize our Azure OpenAI credentials and endpoint configurations directly within our secure Fabric Notebook execution session.
  • Vectorized UDF Definition: By decorating our function with @pandas_udf("array"), we instruct PySpark that the output column will be structured as an array of floating-point values. The inner function accepts a pandas.Series containing text fragments and dispatches API requests to the text-embedding-ada-002 model.
  • Reading Governed Delta Tables: We invoke spark.read.table("Gold_Lakehouse.CustomerSupportTranscripts") to fetch our curated support transcripts natively from OneLake. Fabric abstracts away underlying ABFSS file paths and partition handling automatically.
  • Distributed Transformation: When we execute withColumn("VectorEmbedding", generate_embeddings(...)), PySpark distributes the workload across the active Spark cluster nodes. Each executor node processes a slice of the dataset in parallel, sending batched requests to Azure OpenAI.
  • Atomic Delta Lake Persistence: Finally, we persist the vectorized DataFrame back into OneLake using .write.format("delta").saveAsTable("Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors"). Because Delta Lake provides strict ACID transaction guarantees, our vectorized dataset remains resilient against partial failures during write operations.
Vector Search: Querying Embeddings Using PySpark & Math Functions

Once our text embeddings are persisted in OneLake, we require a method to identify the most relevant customer transcripts when an incoming user query arrives. In traditional RAG setups, this step relies on dedicated vector databases using index structures like HNSW or IVF. However, for datasets containing hundreds of thousands to millions of rows, we can compute mathematical similarity directly within PySpark using vector geometry.

Cosine similarity is the gold standard metric for measuring semantic closeness between high-dimensional text embeddings. Conceptually, it evaluates the angle between two vectors, such as an incoming user query and a stored document to determine how similar they are in context.

Distributed Vector Lookup in PySpark

We can implement this similarity lookup natively by taking an incoming user prompt, generating its vector representation, and computing the dot product against our vector column stored in Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors:

# PySpark Vector Retrieval Code
import numpy as np
from pyspark.sql.functions import udf, col
from pyspark.sql.types import FloatType

# 1. Generate query embedding for user prompt
user_prompt = "How do I reset my customer portal password?"
prompt_response = openai.Embedding.create(input=user_prompt, engine="text-embedding-ada-002")
query_vector = prompt_response['data'][0]['embedding']

# 2. Define a cosine similarity / dot product UDF
@udf(returnType=FloatType())
def compute_similarity(doc_vector):
    if doc_vector is None:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.dot(query_vector, doc_vector))

# 3. Query vectors from OneLake and retrieve top 5 matches
df_vectors = spark.read.table("Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors")
top_matches = (
    df_vectors
    .withColumn("Similarity", compute_similarity(col("VectorEmbedding")))
    .orderBy(col("Similarity").desc())
    .limit(5)
)

# Collect top context documents
retrieved_docs = [row['TranscriptText'] for row in top_matches.collect()]

By executing this transformation across our Spark cluster, we perform candidate vector retrieval directly inside our analytical Lakehouse engine. The process retrieves the most contextually relevant transcript segments within milliseconds, perfectly preparing our pipeline for the generative synthesis stage.

Serving and Orchestration: Synthesizing Context and Deployment

With our vector retrieval engine operational, the final component of our enterprise RAG pipeline is prompt orchestration and response generation. We synthesize the retrieved transcript passages into a grounded context window and submit the instruction to Azure OpenAI Chat Completions.

# Construct grounded context prompt
context_block = "
---
".join(retrieved_docs)
system_instruction = (
    "We are an AI assistant designed to answer customer support queries based strictly on historic logs. "
    "Use only the provided context to answer the prompt accurately."
)

# Call Azure OpenAI Chat Completion
completion_response = openai.ChatCompletion.create(
    engine="gpt-4",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": system_instruction},
        {"role": "user", "content": f"Context:
{context_block}

Question: {user_prompt}"}
    ]
)
final_answer = completion_response['choices'][0]['message']['content']
print(final_answer)
Deployment Patterns: Gradio and Copilot Studio Integrations

To bring this RAG solution into production and surface it to business stakeholders across our organization, we evaluate two highly effective serving patterns:

  • Embedded Interactive Interfaces in Fabric: For internal prototyping, testing, or technical user interfaces, we can wrap our retrieval and synthesis functions into a lightweight Gradio interface running directly within a Fabric Notebook session. This allows analysts to test context retrieval, adjust hyper-parameters, and evaluate model grounding in real time.
  • Copilot Studio & Semantic Link Orchestration: For enterprise-wide deployment, we can expose our PySpark RAG execution logic as an automated backend endpoint or register our Lakehouse tables within Power BI semantic models using Semantic Link (sempy). Copilot Studio can then query these semantic layers and invoke our underlying vectorized tables seamlessly, providing business users with an AI agent that converses with governed enterprise data in real time.
Production Considerations: Performance, Cost, and Governance

As we transition our concise PySpark RAG pipeline into a continuous production environment, we incorporate several critical engineering practices to maintain operational efficiency and low compute cost:

  • Storage Optimization with V-Order: When saving our vectorized Delta tables in OneLake, we ensure that Microsoft’s proprietary V-Order compression is enabled. V-Order reorganizes Parquet files at write time, dramatically improving memory layout and accelerating downstream read speeds when Spark or SQL engines scan vector arrays.
  • Incremental Embeddings via Change Data Capture (CDC): Rather than re-generating embeddings for our entire dataset during every run, we implement incremental processing using Delta Lake transaction logs. By inspecting modified rows, we only vectorize newly inserted or updated customer transcripts, reducing OpenAI API overhead substantially.
  • Unified Data Governance & Security: Because our embeddings reside within native OneLake Delta tables, they inherit Microsoft Purview governance policies, row-level security, and access controls automatically. Sensitive customer information remains fully safeguarded without requiring complex vector database role-based access configurations.
Conclusion

By unifying our storage layer, distributed compute, vector geometry, and generative AI orchestration within Microsoft Fabric, we eliminate the friction of managing external infrastructure. In under 50 lines of Python code, we constructed a resilient, enterprise-grade RAG pipeline that operates entirely on top of open Delta Parquet tables in OneLake. This architecture keeps our enterprise data fully governed, minimizes total cost of ownership, and accelerates our time-to-value when deploying generative AI solutions. As we continue to advance our data engineering practices, solutions like this demonstrate that powerful enterprise AI does not require overly complex stacks, only the right unified foundation.

items.title: LLMs, Python, and CPUs: Why GPUs Aren’t the Only Game in Town
items.summary: When you fire off a prompt to a modern LLM, you sometimes catch it muttering to itself — “thinking,” “planning tasks,” or that oddly specific “generating Python code.” This article is about that last phrase. We spend an inordinate amount of time obsessing over GPUs, trillion-parameter models, and colossal matrix multiplications. But the reality of how AI actually serves you an answer is more nuanced — and it leans on the humble CPU and a language called Python. Here is why the AI industry relies on Python to bridge the gap between probabilistic guessing and deterministic truth, and why the future of AI hardware may look less like a GPU monoculture and more like a balanced ecosystem. 1. Quick Refresher: How Does an LLM Actually Work? Before we wade into the weeds, let’s trace the pipeline using a simple prompt: “What is the capital of France?” 1. Tokenizer: Turns the string (“What is the capital of France?”) into numerical IDs. 2. Embedding: Gives those IDs geographic, semantic, or conceptual meaning. 3. Positional Encoding: Marks the order of words so the model understands sentence structure. 4. Attention: Dynamically links “capital” to “France,” grasping the relationship. 5. Feedforward: Accesses the model’s internal “database” of learned knowledge. 6. Softmax: Determines among the various responses there is a 78% chance the first response word is “Paris,” and outputs it. Under the hood, every single step of this pipeline is driven by massive mathematical operations called matrix multiplications. GPUs are essentially giant calculators fine-tuned to perform these at blistering speed. This architecture is incredible for semantic mapping and predicting language. But what happens when you ask the LLM to do actual math? 2. The Mathematical Limits of Matrix Multiplications Ask an LLM to multiply 45,183 by 9,281, and it won’t “calculate” the answer the way a calculator does. At its core, the raw LLM flow is just a massive sequence of matrix multiplications. These matrices are designed for pattern recognition and probabilistic prediction, not exact calculation. There are three fundamental reasons why pure matrix math struggles with deterministic tasks: Softmax and Loss of Precision: During self-attention, outputs are passed through a softmax function, converting raw scores into probabilities. The network is fundamentally guessing the most statistically likely next token. If you ask it to multiply large numbers, it will output the number that looks most plausible based on its training data — hence the hallucinations. The “One-Pass” Bottleneck: An LLM processes tokens step-by-step. For each token, the input undergoes a fixed number of layers. If a problem requires 100 iterative loops to solve, the LLM cannot “pause” and run extra internal matrix multiplications. It has a constant depth of computation per token. Lack of Working Memory: Matrix multiplications transform vectors in place. An LLM has no physical RAM or CPU registers to store intermediate variables. If it makes a tiny arithmetic mistake early in a chain of thought, that error gets baked into its context window and cascades into total failure. How a Vector ‘Holds’ a Math Concept? But wait, if matrices are so bad at math, how does the LLM do the math it is good at? You have to stop thinking of numbers as text symbols and start thinking of them as geometric locations. Imagine a simplified 3D vector space where the axes represent abstract properties: * X-Axis: Magnitude (How big is it?) * Y-Axis: Parity (Is it even or odd?) * Z-Axis: Prime Status (Is it prime?) In this space, the number “4” isn’t a text character; it’s a spatial coordinate: `[Magnitude: 4.0, Parity: 1.0 (Even), Prime: -1.0 (No)]`. When the LLM processes 4 + 3, its internal patterns perform a geometric transformation. The vector shifts along the X-axis by the magnitude of the second number, and the Y-axis flips (because Even + Odd = Odd). The resulting coordinate lands near [Magnitude: 7.0, Parity: -1.0 (Odd)], which the model then translates back into the text token “7.” This geometric intuition works beautifully for simple concepts, but it breaks down under the weight of complex, multi-step arithmetic. For that, we need a different tool. 3. Why We Delegate to Python To solve the limitations of pure matrix math, modern AI uses a paradigm called Program-Aided Language Models (PAL). Instead of forcing the LLM to be the computer, we use the LLM as a translator that writes instructions for an actual computer. Think of it as a division of labor: The LLM (Matrix Multiplications): Acts as the brain. It is creative, understands natural language, and knows how to solve a problem conceptually. The Python Interpreter (Symbolic Executor): Acts as the calculator. It executes instructions with perfect, cold, mathematical precision. Inside the LLM, specialized attention mechanisms learn to bind entities to attributes — linking variable “x” to “number of grapes” from a word problem, for instance — without needing physical RAM. Once the model has mapped the logic, it outputs the syntax as a Python script and hands off the execution. 4. How is Python Code Generated by an LLM? An LLM doesn’t just guess when to run Python. It executes a highly engineered process: 1. The Setup:The host platform registers a “Tool Box” definition via a silent JSON schema, telling the LLM it has access to a secure Python sandbox. 2. Tool-Call Fine-Tuning: Models undergo training where they learn to recognize intent. If you ask for a poem, it uses standard generation. If you ask it to plot a bar chart from a CSV, it recognizes this requires deterministic execution. 3. The Trigger:If a tool is needed, the LLM halts text generation and outputs a specialized system token, like “ print(45183 * 9281) ”. 4. The Execution Loop: The host platform intercepts this token, sends the code to a secure Docker container, runs it, and feeds the exact output back to the LLM. The LLM then wakes up to format the final answer for the user. 5. Was the Python Sandbox Always There? Before mid-2023, LLMs were purely “minds in a jar” — all matrix multiplication, with no physical hands to touch the outside world. Today’s hybrid sandbox systems bridged that gap. Setting up a Python sandbox is a security and operational nightmare. Without rigorous sandboxing — using isolated virtualization layers with zero network access and strict CPU limits — a malicious user could trick the AI into hosting a botnet or attacking the host server. Furthermore, keeping millions of virtual environments spun up and ready for real-time execution is a massive cloud infrastructure challenge. It took providers like OpenAI and Google significant engineering to make these environments fast, safe, and scalable. 6. Why Python and Not Some Other Language? If we just need a deterministic calculator, why not delegate to C++, Rust, or JavaScript? The industry selected Python for a combination of practical, historical, and technical reasons: The Lingua Franca of AI: Python is the native language of data science. Libraries like NumPy, Pandas, and Matplotlib are already baked into the ecosystem. If an LLM needs to analyze data or draw a chart, Python is the obvious choice. Training Data Abundance: LLMs are trained on the internet, and the internet is overflowing with Python code from GitHub, Stack Overflow, and tutorials. Because the model has seen millions of Python examples, its “Syntax Circuits” are incredibly reliable at generating valid Python without compilation errors. Readability: Python’s indentation-based, highly readable syntax makes it structurally easier for a next-token predictor to generate correctly compared to the bracket-heavy, verbose syntax of languages like Java or C++. But how often are we actually asking these models to write Python versus, say, a sonnet? Let’s look at how this division of labor translates to real-world cloud traffic. 7. The Great Compute Divide: How Much Work Goes Where? While AI companies keep exact telemetry close to their chest, industry analyses reveal a fascinating computational paradox. Today, roughly 20–30% of prompts are strictly CPU-centric, 60–70% are GPU-native, and about 5–10% are hybrid — where a GPU generates code that a CPU then executes. The “CPU-Capable” Overkill (20–30%) : Extracting emails from text, converting CSVs to JSON, or sorting lists. A CPU could process 100,000 of these a second. Instead, we fire up billion-dollar GPU clusters to figure out if a user wants a comma removed. The True “GPU-Native” Tasks (60–70%): Summarizing legal PDFs, drafting polite emails, or brainstorming. You cannot write a Python `if/then` statement for “politeness.” This strictly requires high-dimensional reasoning. The Hybrid / Tool-Use (5–10%): “Analyze this spreadsheet and find the standard deviation.” The GPU understands the request and writes the code; the CPU crunches the numbers. If we look at the actual latency telemetry for a modern “hybrid” prompt — say, asking an AI to analyze a CSV and calculate the standard deviation — the time split is staggering. The LLM running on the GPU takes roughly 4 to 6 seconds just to reason through the request and generate the Python code token-by-token. The CPU then takes about 50 milliseconds to actually execute the code and crunch the numbers. Today, the GPU does 90% of the “thinking time,” while the CPU does 10% of the work but delivers 100% of the mathematical accuracy. Using a 100-billion-parameter GPU cluster to write a script that a CPU executes in a fraction of a second is, frankly, an economic dead end. The industry is acutely aware of this latency bottleneck, which is why architectures are shifting toward semantic routing and code caching — bypassing the GPU generation step for routine tasks. 8. Speculating the Future: A Tiered Compute Ecosystem Today, roughly 70% of AI tasks require true, GPU-native reasoning. But in the future, that 70% will not all be routed to expensive cloud data centers. Instead, workloads will fragment through smart routing, edge migration, and semantic caching. This shift isn’t just a neat architectural trick; it is an absolute necessity driven by physical infrastructure limits. Data center GPU racks can demand upwards of 60kW of power — nearly ten times the draw of a standard CPU rack — and generate immense heat that strains local power grids. Consequently, new data center construction is facing heavy environmental pushback from municipalities. While GPUs are highly efficient at parallel matrix math, using them to execute sequential control logic or basic Python scripts wastes massive amounts of electricity. CPUs, built specifically for sequential tasks, handle deterministic code execution with vastly less energy. Furthermore, we will see the rise of Semantic Code Caching. Right now, every time a user asks for a specific data transformation, the GPU generates the Python code from scratch. In the near future, user prompts will go through an initial semantic search phase. If an LLM has already written a successful script to extract specific metrics from a standard sales report, that code will be sanitized and stored in a central library. Instead of regenerating the code, the LLM simply selects the pre-generated Python script and runs it. This bypasses the expensive GPU generation step entirely for routine tasks, shifting the load to the CPU for retrieval and execution. If we model how today’s traffic will distribute across a tiered hardware ecosystem in the coming years, a plausible, balanced split emerges: Tier 1: Cloud GPUs (Frontier Models) — ~30% of Traffic: This handles the hardest puzzles. Complex multi-step reasoning, deep “System 2” thinking, and continuous Reinforcement Learning training. A portion of today’s 70% GPU-native workload will stay here, but cloud GPUs will transition from basic chatbot hosts into specialized reasoning engines that spend minutes or hours thinking through novel, complex problems (like discovering a new drug for cancer) or writing code for a task that has never been attempted before. Tier 2: Local GPUs & NPUs (Edge Devices) — ~30% of Traffic: Another large chunk of today’s 70% GPU-native workload will move to the edge. Chips like Apple’s M-series and mobile Neural Processing Units (NPUs) have enough unified memory to run highly capable Small Language Models (SLMs) locally. This handles routine semantic tasks, like drafting an email or summarizing a webpage, without ever hitting the cloud. Tier 3: Cloud CPUs (Execution & Retrieval) — ~20% of Traffic: This absorbs the 5–10% of today’s hybrid tool-use tasks, supercharged by caching. Running millions of concurrent, sandboxed Python environments — whether executing newly generated code or retrieving and running cached scripts — requires cloud CPU clusters. The semantic search phase used to find cached scripts relies on vector databases, which are CPU-bound for fast retrieval. Tier 4: Local/Desktop CPUs — ~20% of Traffic: Handling deterministic, rule-based tasks that don’t even need a neural network — like extracting text via regex, sorting local files, or basic arithmetic — will be routed directly to the user’s local CPU in milliseconds. In this new paradigm, GPUs aren’t going away; their role is just maturing. By combining smart semantic routing, localized edge inference, and code caching, the industry will move to an optimized, balanced compute architecture. Summary The LLM acts as the creative brain, parsing messy human intent and formulating a plan, while the traditional CPU acts as the executor, running deterministic Python code with absolute precision. As we look to a future where AI is woven into the fabric of our daily computing, the harmony between the probabilistic GPU and the deterministic CPU will be our guiding principle. Isaac Asimov once said “Part of the inhumanity of the computer is that, once it is competently programmed and working smoothly, it is completely honest.” The LLM may be brilliantly creative, but when we need the absolute truth, Asimov reminds us that we still rely on the cold, completely honest precision of the CPU. items.summary_html:
When you fire off a prompt to a modern LLM, you sometimes catch it muttering to itself — “thinking,” “planning tasks,” or that oddly specific “generating Python code.” This article is about that last phrase. We spend an inordinate amount of time obsessing over GPUs, trillion-parameter models, and colossal matrix multiplications. But the reality of how AI actually serves you an answer is more nuanced — and it leans on the humble CPU and a language called Python.

Here is why the AI industry relies on Python to bridge the gap between probabilistic guessing and deterministic truth, and why the future of AI hardware may look less like a GPU monoculture and more like a balanced ecosystem.

1. Quick Refresher: How Does an LLM Actually Work?

Before we wade into the weeds, let’s trace the pipeline using a simple prompt: “What is the capital of France?”

1. Tokenizer: Turns the string (“What is the capital of France?”) into numerical IDs.

2. Embedding: Gives those IDs geographic, semantic, or conceptual meaning.

3. Positional Encoding: Marks the order of words so the model understands sentence structure.

4. Attention: Dynamically links “capital” to “France,” grasping the relationship.

5. Feedforward: Accesses the model’s internal “database” of learned knowledge.

6. Softmax: Determines among the various responses there is a 78% chance the first response word is “Paris,” and outputs it.

Under the hood, every single step of this pipeline is driven by massive mathematical operations called matrix multiplications. GPUs are essentially giant calculators fine-tuned to perform these at blistering speed. This architecture is incredible for semantic mapping and predicting language. But what happens when you ask the LLM to do actual math?

2. The Mathematical Limits of Matrix Multiplications

Ask an LLM to multiply 45,183 by 9,281, and it won’t “calculate” the answer the way a calculator does. At its core, the raw LLM flow is just a massive sequence of matrix multiplications. These matrices are designed for pattern recognition and probabilistic prediction, not exact calculation.

There are three fundamental reasons why pure matrix math struggles with deterministic tasks:

Softmax and Loss of Precision: During self-attention, outputs are passed through a softmax function, converting raw scores into probabilities. The network is fundamentally guessing the most statistically likely next token. If you ask it to multiply large numbers, it will output the number that looks most plausible based on its training data — hence the hallucinations.

The “One-Pass” Bottleneck: An LLM processes tokens step-by-step. For each token, the input undergoes a fixed number of layers. If a problem requires 100 iterative loops to solve, the LLM cannot “pause” and run extra internal matrix multiplications. It has a constant depth of computation per token.

Lack of Working Memory: Matrix multiplications transform vectors in place. An LLM has no physical RAM or CPU registers to store intermediate variables. If it makes a tiny arithmetic mistake early in a chain of thought, that error gets baked into its context window and cascades into total failure.

How a Vector ‘Holds’ a Math Concept?

But wait, if matrices are so bad at math, how does the LLM do the math it is good at? You have to stop thinking of numbers as text symbols and start thinking of them as geometric locations.

Imagine a simplified 3D vector space where the axes represent abstract properties:

* X-Axis: Magnitude (How big is it?)

* Y-Axis: Parity (Is it even or odd?)

* Z-Axis: Prime Status (Is it prime?)

In this space, the number “4” isn’t a text character; it’s a spatial coordinate: `[Magnitude: 4.0, Parity: 1.0 (Even), Prime: -1.0 (No)]`.

When the LLM processes 4 + 3, its internal patterns perform a geometric transformation. The vector shifts along the X-axis by the magnitude of the second number, and the Y-axis flips (because Even + Odd = Odd). The resulting coordinate lands near [Magnitude: 7.0, Parity: -1.0 (Odd)], which the model then translates back into the text token “7.”

This geometric intuition works beautifully for simple concepts, but it breaks down under the weight of complex, multi-step arithmetic. For that, we need a different tool.

3. Why We Delegate to Python

To solve the limitations of pure matrix math, modern AI uses a paradigm called Program-Aided Language Models (PAL). Instead of forcing the LLM to be the computer, we use the LLM as a translator that writes instructions for an actual computer.

Think of it as a division of labor:

The LLM (Matrix Multiplications): Acts as the brain. It is creative, understands natural language, and knows how to solve a problem conceptually.

The Python Interpreter (Symbolic Executor): Acts as the calculator. It executes instructions with perfect, cold, mathematical precision.

Inside the LLM, specialized attention mechanisms learn to bind entities to attributes — linking variable “x” to “number of grapes” from a word problem, for instance — without needing physical RAM. Once the model has mapped the logic, it outputs the syntax as a Python script and hands off the execution.

4. How is Python Code Generated by an LLM?

An LLM doesn’t just guess when to run Python. It executes a highly engineered process:

1. The Setup:The host platform registers a “Tool Box” definition via a silent JSON schema, telling the LLM it has access to a secure Python sandbox.

2. Tool-Call Fine-Tuning: Models undergo training where they learn to recognize intent. If you ask for a poem, it uses standard generation. If you ask it to plot a bar chart from a CSV, it recognizes this requires deterministic execution.

3. The Trigger:If a tool is needed, the LLM halts text generation and outputs a specialized system token, like “print(45183 * 9281)”.

4. The Execution Loop: The host platform intercepts this token, sends the code to a secure Docker container, runs it, and feeds the exact output back to the LLM. The LLM then wakes up to format the final answer for the user.

5. Was the Python Sandbox Always There?

Before mid-2023, LLMs were purely “minds in a jar” — all matrix multiplication, with no physical hands to touch the outside world. Today’s hybrid sandbox systems bridged that gap.

Setting up a Python sandbox is a security and operational nightmare. Without rigorous sandboxing — using isolated virtualization layers with zero network access and strict CPU limits — a malicious user could trick the AI into hosting a botnet or attacking the host server. Furthermore, keeping millions of virtual environments spun up and ready for real-time execution is a massive cloud infrastructure challenge. It took providers like OpenAI and Google significant engineering to make these environments fast, safe, and scalable.

6. Why Python and Not Some Other Language?

If we just need a deterministic calculator, why not delegate to C++, Rust, or JavaScript?

The industry selected Python for a combination of practical, historical, and technical reasons:

The Lingua Franca of AI: Python is the native language of data science. Libraries like NumPy, Pandas, and Matplotlib are already baked into the ecosystem. If an LLM needs to analyze data or draw a chart, Python is the obvious choice.

Training Data Abundance: LLMs are trained on the internet, and the internet is overflowing with Python code from GitHub, Stack Overflow, and tutorials. Because the model has seen millions of Python examples, its “Syntax Circuits” are incredibly reliable at generating valid Python without compilation errors.

Readability: Python’s indentation-based, highly readable syntax makes it structurally easier for a next-token predictor to generate correctly compared to the bracket-heavy, verbose syntax of languages like Java or C++.

But how often are we actually asking these models to write Python versus, say, a sonnet? Let’s look at how this division of labor translates to real-world cloud traffic.

7. The Great Compute Divide: How Much Work Goes Where?

While AI companies keep exact telemetry close to their chest, industry analyses reveal a fascinating computational paradox. Today, roughly 20–30% of prompts are strictly CPU-centric, 60–70% are GPU-native, and about 5–10% are hybrid — where a GPU generates code that a CPU then executes.

  • The “CPU-Capable” Overkill (20–30%):Extracting emails from text, converting CSVs to JSON, or sorting lists. A CPU could process 100,000 of these a second. Instead, we fire up billion-dollar GPU clusters to figure out if a user wants a comma removed.
  • The True “GPU-Native” Tasks (60–70%):Summarizing legal PDFs, drafting polite emails, or brainstorming. You cannot write a Python `if/then` statement for “politeness.” This strictly requires high-dimensional reasoning.
  • The Hybrid / Tool-Use (5–10%): “Analyze this spreadsheet and find the standard deviation.” The GPU understands the request and writes the code; the CPU crunches the numbers.

If we look at the actual latency telemetry for a modern “hybrid” prompt — say, asking an AI to analyze a CSV and calculate the standard deviation — the time split is staggering. The LLM running on the GPU takes roughly 4 to 6 seconds just to reason through the request and generate the Python code token-by-token. The CPU then takes about 50 milliseconds to actually execute the code and crunch the numbers. Today, the GPU does 90% of the “thinking time,” while the CPU does 10% of the work but delivers 100% of the mathematical accuracy.

Using a 100-billion-parameter GPU cluster to write a script that a CPU executes in a fraction of a second is, frankly, an economic dead end. The industry is acutely aware of this latency bottleneck, which is why architectures are shifting toward semantic routing and code caching — bypassing the GPU generation step for routine tasks.

8. Speculating the Future: A Tiered Compute Ecosystem

Today, roughly 70% of AI tasks require true, GPU-native reasoning. But in the future, that 70% will not all be routed to expensive cloud data centers. Instead, workloads will fragment through smart routing, edge migration, and semantic caching.

This shift isn’t just a neat architectural trick; it is an absolute necessity driven by physical infrastructure limits. Data center GPU racks can demand upwards of 60kW of power — nearly ten times the draw of a standard CPU rack — and generate immense heat that strains local power grids. Consequently, new data center construction is facing heavy environmental pushback from municipalities. While GPUs are highly efficient at parallel matrix math, using them to execute sequential control logic or basic Python scripts wastes massive amounts of electricity. CPUs, built specifically for sequential tasks, handle deterministic code execution with vastly less energy.

Furthermore, we will see the rise of Semantic Code Caching. Right now, every time a user asks for a specific data transformation, the GPU generates the Python code from scratch. In the near future, user prompts will go through an initial semantic search phase. If an LLM has already written a successful script to extract specific metrics from a standard sales report, that code will be sanitized and stored in a central library. Instead of regenerating the code, the LLM simply selects the pre-generated Python script and runs it. This bypasses the expensive GPU generation step entirely for routine tasks, shifting the load to the CPU for retrieval and execution.

If we model how today’s traffic will distribute across a tiered hardware ecosystem in the coming years, a plausible, balanced split emerges:

Tier 1: Cloud GPUs (Frontier Models) — ~30% of Traffic: This handles the hardest puzzles. Complex multi-step reasoning, deep “System 2” thinking, and continuous Reinforcement Learning training. A portion of today’s 70% GPU-native workload will stay here, but cloud GPUs will transition from basic chatbot hosts into specialized reasoning engines that spend minutes or hours thinking through novel, complex problems (like discovering a new drug for cancer) or writing code for a task that has never been attempted before.

Tier 2: Local GPUs & NPUs (Edge Devices) — ~30% of Traffic: Another large chunk of today’s 70% GPU-native workload will move to the edge. Chips like Apple’s M-series and mobile Neural Processing Units (NPUs) have enough unified memory to run highly capable Small Language Models (SLMs) locally. This handles routine semantic tasks, like drafting an email or summarizing a webpage, without ever hitting the cloud.

Tier 3: Cloud CPUs (Execution & Retrieval) — ~20% of Traffic: This absorbs the 5–10% of today’s hybrid tool-use tasks, supercharged by caching. Running millions of concurrent, sandboxed Python environments — whether executing newly generated code or retrieving and running cached scripts — requires cloud CPU clusters. The semantic search phase used to find cached scripts relies on vector databases, which are CPU-bound for fast retrieval.

Tier 4: Local/Desktop CPUs — ~20% of Traffic: Handling deterministic, rule-based tasks that don’t even need a neural network — like extracting text via regex, sorting local files, or basic arithmetic — will be routed directly to the user’s local CPU in milliseconds.

In this new paradigm, GPUs aren’t going away; their role is just maturing. By combining smart semantic routing, localized edge inference, and code caching, the industry will move to an optimized, balanced compute architecture.

Summary

The LLM acts as the creative brain, parsing messy human intent and formulating a plan, while the traditional CPU acts as the executor, running deterministic Python code with absolute precision. As we look to a future where AI is woven into the fabric of our daily computing, the harmony between the probabilistic GPU and the deterministic CPU will be our guiding principle. Isaac Asimov once said

“Part of the inhumanity of the computer is that, once it is competently programmed and working smoothly, it is completely honest.”

The LLM may be brilliantly creative, but when we need the absolute truth, Asimov reminds us that we still rely on the cold, completely honest precision of the CPU.

items.title: Your Requirements Doc Is 400 Pages Long. Your AI Agent Just Gave Up.
items.summary: Here is a scene a lot of QA testers know too well: You open GitHub Copilot Chat (or whatever AI coding assistant you use), paste in your massive requirements document, and type: “Generate test cases for the login and payment flow.” Copilot chews on it for a second, and then: It times out or throws a “context window exceeded” error. It gives you generic, superficial test cases that clearly skipped 90% of your actual acceptance criteria. It crawls at a snail’s pace because it is reading hundreds of pages of unneeded text every time you ask a question. If this sounds familiar, you are not doing anything wrong. You just ran headfirst into a fundamental LLM bottleneck: AI agents do not have infinite attention, and stuffing giant documents into their prompt is slow, expensive, and frankly wasteful when all you need is the two paragraphs defining the payment retry rules. The good news? This is a solved problem. Search engines and chatbot engineers have tackled the “needle in a haystack” challenge for years. We can borrow their playbooks. Let’s break down the best practical options — from production-grade to dead simple. The Core Fix: Stop Feeding It Everything The solution across every pattern is the same: search first, generate second. Instead of dumping the encyclopedia into your prompt, pull only the specific slice relevant to the feature you are testing. Hand that exact snippet to Agent alongside your test generation instructions. This approach is known as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) . Less text in means faster responses, fewer tokens billed, and far higher test fidelity because Agent is not hallucinating through 380 pages of irrelevant background info. Let’s look at four ways to set this up. Option 1: Classic Vector RAG (Semantic Search) This is the standard pattern teams talk about when they say “RAG.” How it works: Break your requirements into modular chunks (around 300–500 words each). Convert each chunk into an embedding vector (a mathematical representation of its meaning) using an embedding model. Store those vectors in a lightweight vector store (like Chroma, FAISS, or Pinecone). When you ask: “Write edge cases for checkout failure,” your query is embedded, the database finds chunks with matching semantic meaning, and only those 2–3 chunks are fed into Agent. In Practice: Say your doc covers User Authentication , Payment Processing , Retry and Timeout Rules , and Notification Settings . If you query for payment recovery tests, semantic search identifies Payment Processing and Retry and Timeout Rules as conceptual matches, ignoring everything else. Agent receives 700 words rather than 50,000. When to use: Massive, evolving documentation where your search terms might not match the document word-for-word (e.g., you ask about “declined cards” but the doc calls it “unsuccessful transaction processing”). The Catch: Requires spinning up an embedding pipeline, picking a vector store, and running indexing scripts. Great for engineering platforms, but often overkill for a QA engineer who just wants test cases this afternoon. Option 2: Vector-less RAG with BM25 (Smart Keyword Search) You do not actually need vectors or GPUs to do retrieval. Good old-fashioned probabilistic keyword search works remarkably well. BM25 is the battle-tested ranking algorithm powering enterprise search tools like Elasticsearch. It scores text chunks based on keyword frequency, but balances that by down-weighting terms that appear everywhere and rewarding chunks that contain rare, specific terms. How it works: Split your documents into individual section files. Index them locally with a small library like rank-bm25. Query the index using your test prompt keywords. Feed the top 2 ranked files directly into Agent. In Practice: You ask for “test scenarios for OTP timeout lockout.” BM25 looks across your files, flags files containing the exact tokens OTP, timeout, and lockout, and instantly surfaces auth_otp_spec.md. No embeddings, no external API costs, and it runs in less than 20 lines of Python. When to use: Highly technical requirements where QA engineers naturally query with the exact terms defined in the spec. The Catch: Zero tolerance for synonyms. If the spec says “abort transaction” and you search for “cancel payment,” BM25 will score it lower because the exact tokens do not match. Option 3: Structured Chunking + Keyword Index JSON This is the lightweight, zero-infra approach. It gives you full control and works natively inside VS Code with GitHub Copilot Chat. Instead of arbitrary word-count splits that cut sentences in half, we chunk logically by Markdown headings (#, ##, or ###). Each section becomes its own bite-sized file, accompanied by a generated keyword index. Automated Chunking with Python (Bag-of-Words) Here is a clean Python script that splits a requirements document on Markdown headers, extracts the most prominent non-trivial keywords (bag-of-words), and writes an index JSON: import os import re import json from collections import Counter STOPWORDS = { "the", "and", "for", "with", "that", "this", "from", "are", "user", "system", "shall", "must", "will", "should", "when" } def chunk_by_markdown_headers(markdown_text): # Split on lines starting with ## or ### sections = re.split(r'(?m)(?=^#{2,3}\s+)', markdown_text) return [s.strip() for s in sections if s.strip()] def extract_keywords(text, top_n=6): words = re.findall(r'[a-zA-Z]{3,}', text.lower()) filtered = [w for w in words if w not in STOPWORDS] counts = Counter(filtered) return [word for word, _ in counts.most_common(top_n)] def build_index(doc_path, output_dir="chunks"): os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True) with open(doc_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f: content = f.read() chunks = chunk_by_markdown_headers(content) index = [] for i, chunk in enumerate(chunks, 1): first_line = chunk.splitlines()[0].replace("#", "").strip() filename = f"chunk_{i:02d}_{re.sub(r'\W+', '_', first_line).lower()}.md" filepath = os.path.join(output_dir, filename) with open(filepath, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f: f.write(chunk) index.append({ "chunk_id": i, "title": first_line, "file": filepath, "keywords": extract_keywords(chunk) }) with open(os.path.join(output_dir, "requirements_index.json"), "w") as f: json.dump(index, f, indent=2) return index if __name__ == "__main__": build_index("system_requirements.md") What the Generated Index Looks Like: [ { "chunk_id": 1, "title": "User Authentication and OTP", "file": "chunks/chunk_01_user_authentication_and_otp.md", "keywords": ["password", "lockout", "biometric", "expiry", "session", "token"] }, { "chunk_id": 2, "title": "Payment Processing and Retries", "file": "chunks/chunk_02_payment_processing_and_retries.md", "keywords": ["gateway", "refund", "stripe", "timeout", "reversal", "invoice"] } ] The Copilot Power Move: #file Variable Once your docs are chunked into your repository or test workspace, you do not have to copy and paste anything. In GitHub Copilot Chat, you can reference the specific chunk directly using the #file variable: “Using #file:chunks/chunk_02_payment_processing_and_retries.md, generate positive and negative boundary test cases for transaction timeouts.” Copilot pulls only that file into memory, keeping token counts minimal, execution immediate, and hallucination rates near zero. Option 4: Ditch Binary Files — Use CSVs and Markdown Instead of Excel and Word A hidden reason AI assistants choke on requirements is the format. Binary formats like .xlsx and .docx are zipped archives packed with XML trees, styling tags, font references, cell bounds, and metadata. When an LLM or extension tries to extract their contents, token counters spike just to parse the structural bloat. Plain text formats like .csv and .md eliminate all formatting overhead: For Massive Word Docs: Export or convert them directly to Markdown (.md). Markdown headers cleanly translate to test hierarchy markers, making chunking automatic. For Massive Multi-Sheet Workbooks: Avoid feeding an entire 15-tab workbook to the model. Break the workbook down by saving each worksheet as an independent CSV file. Indexing Multiple CSV Worksheets Pair your exported worksheet CSVs with an explicit mapping index: { "worksheets": [ { "file": "specs/auth_matrix.csv", "module": "Authentication & Access Control", "keywords": ["roles", "rbac", "permissions", "admin", "token_refresh"] }, { "file": "specs/payment_gateways.csv", "module": "Payment Gateway Integration", "keywords": ["webhook", "settlement", "idempotency", "currency_conversion"] }, { "file": "specs/error_codes.csv", "module": "Error Code Definitions", "keywords": ["http_500", "retry_after", "rate_limit", "unauthorized"] } ] } Whenever you need tests for token refresh or RBAC, you load auth_matrix.csv alone. Copilot receives clean tabular rows with zero XML luggage. Decision Guide: Which One Fits Your Team? Enterprise test suite with thousands of pages & varying jargon → Best approach : Classic Vector RAG → Why : Finds conceptual matches even when test prompt words don’t match document terms. Strict technical specifications with standardized vocabulary → Best approach : Vector-less BM25 → Why : Near-instant retrieval, 100% local, zero embedding pipeline costs. Individual QA tester working locally in VS Code / IDE → Best approach : Heading Chunking + Index JSON → Why : Simplest execution. Use #file in Copilot Chat for precise context targeting. Legacy requirements stuck in heavy Word or Excel documents → Best approach : CSV / Markdown Conversion → Why : Baseline necessity. Cuts 60–80% of token bloat before applying any search method.
